28:19.body: Bahya asks why we need the old name לוז, and answers that it is also a bone in the spine, linked to the dead rising again. Rashbam says the city took the name Bethel from the spot outside it where Jacob slept.

sources.quote: מִלְּשׁוֹן ״לוּז הַשִּׁדְרָה״ בָּאָדָם, שֶׁמִּמֶּנּוּ עָתִיד לְהִתְנַעֵר וּלְהִתְחַדֵּשׁ וּלְהִבָּרֵא לִתְחִיַּת הַמֵּתִים
sources.says: Bahya says the name לוז comes from the לוז of the human spine, from which a person is to be renewed at the revival of the dead.

sources.quote: ועל שם המקום שחוץ לעיר ששכב יעקב, נקרא שם העיר עצמה בית אל
sources.says: Rashbam says the city itself was named Bethel after the place outside the city where Jacob lay.

28:21.headline: 'In peace' may mean 'without sin' or 'with a family'
28:21.body: Rashi reads בשלום as whole, free of sin, so Jacob does not pick up Laban's ways. Radak reads it as returning with a wife and children, since without them there is no peace.

sources.quote: שָׁלֵם מִן הַחֵטְא, שֶׁלֹּא אֶלְמַד מִדַּרְכֵי לָבָן
sources.says: Rashi says it means whole from sin, so that Jacob will not learn from Laban's ways.

sources.quote: בְּאִשָּׁה וּבְבָנִים, כִּי זוּלָתָם לֹא יִהְיֶה שָׁלוֹם לוֹ וְלֹא לְאָבִיו וְלֹא לְאִמּוֹ
sources.says: Radak says it means with a wife and children, since without them there would be no peace for him, his father or his mother.

29:6.headline: בא-ה means 'is coming' here and 'came' in verse 9
29:6.body: The same letters read two ways depending on where the stress falls. Rashi says here the stress is on the last syllable, so Rachel 'is coming', but in verse 9 it is earlier, so she 'came'.

sources.quote: הָרִאשׁוֹן לְשׁוֹן עוֹשָׂה וְהַשֵּׁנִי לְשׁוֹן עָשְׂתָה
sources.says: Rashi says the first one is a present form and the second a past form.

sources.quote: מלרע שהוא תואר השם כמו פועל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the stress here is on the last syllable, which makes it a describing word like 'doer'.

sources.quote: מלעיל והוא פועל עבר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says in verse 9 the stress is on the first syllable and it is a past verb.

29:10.headline: Jacob rolled the huge stone like a bottle cap
29:10.body: The stone was too big for the shepherds to move alone. Rashi says Jacob removed it as easily as a person lifts the stopper from a small bottle, to show how strong he was.

sources.quote: כְּמִי שֶׁמַּעֲבִיר אֶת הַפְּקָק מֵעַל פִּי צְלוֹחִית; לְהוֹדִיעֲךָ שֶׁכֹּחוֹ גָּדוֹל
sources.says: Rashi says he moved it like a person removing the stopper from a small bottle, to show his great strength.

29:13.headline: Laban ran, hugged and kissed, looking for treasure
29:13.body: Rashi reads each of Laban's actions as a search for money. He ran because he thought Jacob carried riches, hugged to feel for gold coins, and kissed to see if pearls were in his mouth.

sources.quote: כַּסָּבוּר מָמוֹן הוּא טָעוּן
sources.says: Rashi says Laban ran because he thought Jacob was carrying money.

sources.quote: כְּשֶׁלֹּא רָאָה עִמּוֹ כְלוּם, אָמַר שֶׁמָּא זְהוּבִים הֵבִיא וְהִנָּם בְּחֵיקוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says that when Laban saw nothing with him, he thought Jacob might have gold coins in his bosom.

sources.quote: אָמַר שֶׁמָּא מַרְגָּלִיוֹת הֵבִיא וְהֵם בְּפִיו
sources.says: Rashi says Laban then thought Jacob might have brought pearls in his mouth.

29:14.headline: אך can mean 'truly' or a cold 'only'
29:14.body: Radak reads Laban's words warmly: 'you truly are my bone and flesh'. Rashi reads them as a limit: since you bring nothing, I will take you in only out of kinship, for a month.

sources.quote: אַךְ עַצְמִי. פֵּרַשׁ: בֶּאֱמֶת, וְכֵן ״אַךְ טוֹב לְיִשְׂרָאֵל אֱלֹהִים
sources.says: Radak says אך means 'truly', as in 'truly God is good to Israel'.

sources.quote: מֵעַתָּה אֵין לִי לְאָסְפְּךָ הַבַּיְתָה, הוֹאִיל וְאֵין בְּיָדְךָ כְלוּם, אֶלָּא מִפְּנֵי קוּרְבָה אֲטַפֵּל בְּךָ חֹדֶש יָמִים
sources.says: Rashi says Laban meant he had no reason to take Jacob in, since he had nothing, but out of kinship he would care for him for a month.

29:15.headline: Is הכי a question or a firm statement?
29:15.body: Rashi reads Laban's הכי as a question of surprise: just because you are my relative, should you work for nothing? Bahya says the word is not a doubt at all but a certainty.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן תֵּמַהּ, וְכִי בִּשְׁבִיל שֶׁאָחִי אַתָּה תַּעַבְדֵנִי חִנָּם
sources.says: Rashi says it is a word of surprise: because you are my brother, will you work for me for free?

sources.quote: מִלַּת ״הֲכִי״ אֵינוֹ לְשׁוֹן מְסֻפָּק רַק לְשׁוֹן וַדַּאי
sources.says: Bahya says the word הכי is not a word of doubt but of certainty.

29:17.headline: רכות may mean 'weak and weeping' or 'lovely'
29:17.body: Rashi says Leah's eyes were weak from crying, since she feared she would be given to Esau, and Radak agrees they were soft and tearful. Rashbam takes the word as 'pretty', and Bahya passes on a view that it means 'long'.

sources.quote: שֶׁהָיְתָה סְבוּרָה לַעֲלוֹת בְּגוֹרָלוֹ שֶׁל עֵשָׂו וּבוֹכָה
sources.says: Rashi says she was weeping because she thought she would fall to Esau's lot.

sources.quote: יְפַת תֹּאַר הָיְתָה, אֶלָּא שֶׁעֵינֶיהָ הָיוּ רַכּוֹת וְדוֹמְעוֹת
sources.says: Radak says she was beautiful but her eyes were soft and teary.

sources.quote: וכלה שעיניה נאות אין כל גופה צריך בדיקה
sources.says: Rashbam takes רכות as 'pretty', and says a bride with lovely eyes needs no further checking.

sources.quote: רַכּוֹת״ חֲסַר אָלֶ״ף, וְטַעְמוֹ ״אֲרֻכּוֹת
sources.says: Bahya quotes a view that רכות is missing an aleph and means ארכות, 'long'.

29:27.headline: ונתנה could be 'we will give' or 'she will be given'
29:27.body: Rashi says Laban speaks in the plural, 'we will give you', and Chizkuni says he spoke for the townspeople because Jacob no longer trusted him. Radak adds that it may be a passive form, 'she will be given to you'.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן רַבִּים, כְּמוֹ נֵרְדָה וְנָבְלָה וְנִשְׂרְפָה
sources.says: Rashi says it is a plural form, like 'let us go down' and 'let us burn'.

sources.quote: לשון רבים לפי שמתחלה רימהו לבן ליעקב ולא היה יעקב מאמינו עד שהבטיחוהו עכשיו אנשי המקום
sources.says: Chizkuni says the plural is because Laban had cheated Jacob at first and Jacob would not trust him until the townspeople promised.

sources.quote: יִתָּכֵן שֶׁהַמִּלָּה מִבִּנְיַן נִפְעַל לִנְקֵבָה
sources.says: Radak says the word may be a passive form for a woman, meaning she will be given.

29:33.headline: שמעון comes from 'the LORD heard'
29:33.body: The verse ties the name to 'the LORD heard' that Leah was unloved. Radak says it means He heard her prayer, and the sages read it as 'one who listens to his Father in heaven'.

sources.quote: שָׁמַע לִתְפִלָּתִי וּתְחִנָּתִי
sources.says: Radak says it means He heard my prayer and my plea.

sources.quote: שִׁמְעוֹן, שׁוֹמֵעַ בְּקוֹל אָבִיו שֶׁבַּשָּׁמָיִם
sources.says: Bereshit Rabbah reads שמעון as one who listens to the voice of his Father in heaven.

29:34.headline: לוי comes from ילוה, 'will be joined'
29:34.body: Leah says her husband will now be joined to her, since she has borne him three sons, and Ibn Ezra links ילוה to a verb for joining. The sages add that Levi would one day join the children to their Father in heaven.

sources.quote: ילוה אישי. כמו "ונלוו עליך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says ילוה is like 'they shall be joined to you'.

sources.quote: יִהְיֶה נִלְוֶה לְאַהֲבָתִי יוֹתֵר מֵאַהֲבַת אֲחוֹתִי
sources.says: Radak says he will be joined to her love more than to her sister's love.

sources.quote: לֵוִי זֶה עָתִיד לְלַוּוֹת אֶת הַבָּנִים לַאֲבִיהֶן שֶׁבַּשָּׁמַיִם
sources.says: Bereshit Rabbah says Levi was destined to accompany the children to their Father in heaven.

29:35.headline: יהודה holds the letters of God's name and means 'thanks'
29:35.body: Leah says she will give thanks, אודה, and names him יהודה. Sforno notes the name holds the letters of the divine Name and also means thanks, and Rashi says Leah owed thanks for receiving more than her share.

sources.quote: שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּזֶה הַשֵּׁם אוֹתִיּוֹת הַשֵּׁם הַנִּכְבָּד, וְעִם זֶה לְשׁוֹן הַהוֹדָאָה
sources.says: Sforno says this name contains the letters of the honored Name, and also carries the sense of giving thanks.

sources.quote: שֶׁנָּטַלְתִּי יוֹתֵר מֵחֶלְקִי, מֵעַתָּה יֵשׁ לִי לְהוֹדוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says Leah means: I took more than my share, so now I must give thanks.

3:1.headline: The serpent’s cunning echoes the humans’ nakedness
3:1.body: Ibn Ezra points out the sound play between ערום, “cunning,” and ערומים, “naked,” in the previous verse. The similar words carry different meanings.

sources.quote: ופי' ערום חכם שיעשה דבריו בערמה, ואל תתמה בעבור היות ערום אחר ערומים, והם שני טעמים, כי באלה הצחות בלשון, כמו "בלחי החמור חמור חמורתים (שופ', טו טז), וכן "על שלשים עיירים, ושלשים עיירים להם" (שם יו"ד ד),
sources.says: Ibn Ezra points out a sound play between ערום and ערומים.

3:3.headline: Eve adds a ban on touching the tree
3:3.body: Rashi notices that תגעו, “touch,” adds a restriction God had not given. He says this addition helped lead to breaking the command.

sources.quote: ולא תגעו בו. הוֹסִיפָה עַל הַצִּוּוּי, לְפִיכָךְ בָּאָה לִידֵי גֵרָעוֹן, הוּא שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר אַל תּוֹסְףְּ עַל דְּבָרָיו (משלי ל'):
sources.says: Rashi says Eve’s added restriction helped lead her to break the command.

3:5.headline: Like rulers, or like creators of worlds
3:5.body: Maimonides follows Onkelos in reading כאלהים as “like rulers.” Rashi reads the serpent’s promise as the power to create worlds.

sources.quote: ולפני שאפרט את הקושיה ופתרונה אקדים שכל דובר עברית יודע שהמונח 'אלהים' משותף א) לאלוה ב) ולמלאכים ג) ולשופטים מנהיגי המדינות. וכבר ביאר אנקלוס הגר עליו השלום, ואמת מה שביאר, שבפסוק "וִהְיִיתֶם כֵּאלֹהִים יֹדְעֵי טוֹב וָרָע" (בראשית ג,ה) הכוונה למשמעות האחרונה, ותרגם: "וּתְהוֹן כְּרַבְרְבִין" (=ותהיו כגדולים, כנכבדים).
sources.says: Maimonides says Onkelos understands אלהים here as human judges and rulers.

sources.quote: והייתם כאלהים. יוֹצְרֵי עוֹלָמוֹת (בראשית רבה):
sources.says: Rashi explains the promise as becoming creators of worlds.

3:7.headline: Their eyes open to a new sense of shame
3:7.body: Maimonides says ותפקחנה describes a change in judgment: they now find nakedness shameful. Their eyesight has not changed.

sources.quote: התבונן בנאמר: "וַתִּפָּקַחְנָה עֵינֵי שְׁנֵיהֶם וַיֵּדְעוּ כִּי עֵירֻמִּם הֵם" (בראשית ג,ז). לא נאמר 'ותפקחנה עיני שניהם ויראו', משום שמה שראה לפני כן הוא אשר ראה לאחר מכן. לא היה כיסוי על עיניו שהוסר, אלא נוצר לו מצב אחר, שבו הוא ראה כמגונה מה שלא ראה כמגונה קודם לכן.
sources.says: Maimonides says their sight was unchanged, but nakedness now seemed shameful.

sources.quote: ותפקחנה וגו'. לְעִנְיַן הַחָכְמָה דִּבֵּר הַכָּתוּב וְלֹא לְעִנְיַן רְאִיָּה מַמָּשׁ, וְסוֹף הַמִּקְרָא מוֹכִיחַ:
sources.says: Rashi says the opening concerns understanding rather than physical sight.

3:7.headline: They are also stripped of their one commandment
3:7.body: Rashi asks why nakedness needed to be discovered when even a blind person knows they are naked. He reads עירמם as also meaning that they have lost the one commandment entrusted to them.

sources.quote: וידעו כי עירמים הם. אַף הַסּוּמָא יוֹדֵעַ כְּשֶׁהוּא עָרוּם, אֶלָּא מַהוּ וַיֵּדְעוּ כִּי עֵירֻמִּם הֵם? מִצְוָה אַחַת הָיְתָה בְיָדָם וְנִתְעַרְטְלוּ הֵימֶנָּה (בראשית רבה):
sources.says: Rashi says they had one commandment and were stripped of it.

3:8.headline: The sound is moving through the garden
3:8.body: Maimonides reads מתהלך, “walking,” as describing God’s voice spreading through the garden. The word can describe a sound traveling, without anyone taking steps.

sources.quote: ג) לאחר מכן הושאל להתפשטות דבר כלשהו והופעתו, גם אם אין הוא גשמי כלל. נאמר: "קוֹלָהּ כַּנָּחָשׁ יֵלֵךְ" (ירמיהו מו,כב). וכיוצא בזה דבריו "[וַיִּשְׁמְעוּ אֶת] קוֹל ה' אֱלֹהִים מִתְהַלֵּךְ בַּגָּן" (בראשית ג,ח), הקול הוא שנאמר לגביו שהיה מתהלך.
sources.says: Maimonides says the voice is what the verse describes as moving.

3:8.headline: A direction toward sunset, or the evening breeze
3:8.body: Rashi reads רוח as a direction: west, where the sun sets. Ibn Ezra reads it as the breeze near evening.

sources.quote: לרוח היום. לְאוֹתוֹ רוּחַ שֶׁהַשֶּׁמֶשׁ בָּאָה לְשָׁם, וְזוֹ הִיא מַעֲרָבִית; שֶׁלִּפְנוֹת עֶרֶב חַמָּה בַּמַּעֲרָב, וְהֵם סָרְחוּ בָּעֲשִׂירִית (סנהדרין ל"ח):
sources.says: Rashi reads the phrase as the western direction at the approach of evening.

sources.quote: וישמעו מתהלך בגן., קול השם, וזה היה סמוך לערב בעת התנופף רוח היום,
sources.says: Ibn Ezra places the event near evening when the day’s breeze is blowing.

sources.quote: 2 ב) הוא גם שם הרוח המנשבת: "וְרוּחַ הַקָּדִים נָשָׂא אֶת הָאַרְבֶּה" (שמות י,יג), "רוּחַ יָם" (שם,יט). וזה נפוץ.
sources.says: Maimonides lists a blowing wind as one meaning of רוח.

3:15.headline: Crushing and hissing share the sound of the punishment
3:15.body: Rashi reads ישופך as crushing the serpent’s head, but links תשופנו to the hiss before its bite. He says the verse uses matching sounds for the two attacks.

sources.quote: ישופך. יְכַתֶּתְךָ (סוטה ט') כְּמוֹ וָאֶכֹּת אֹתוֹ (דברים ט), וְתַרְגּוּמוֹ וְשָׁפִית יָתֵי':
sources.says: Rashi explains ישופך as crushing.

sources.quote: ואתה תשופנו עקב. לֹא יְהֵא לְךָ קוֹמָה וְתִשְּׁכֶנּוּ בַּעֲקֵבוֹ, וְאַף מִשָּׁם תְּמִיתֶנּוּ, וּלְשׁוֹן תְּשׁוּפֶנּוּ כְּמוֹ נָשַׁף בָּהֶם (ישעיהו מ') כְּשֶׁהַנָּחָשׁ בָּא לִנְשֹׁך הוּא נוֹשֵׁף כְּמִין שְׁרִיקָה וּלְפִי שֶׁהַלָּשׁוֹן נוֹפֵל עַל הַלָּשָוֹן כְּתִיב לְשׁוֹן נְשִׁיפָה בִשְׁנֵיהֶם:
sources.says: Rashi links תשופנו to a serpent’s hissing and explicitly identifies a play between the two expressions.

3:16.headline: Desire and obedience give two different readings
3:16.body: Ibn Ezra reads תשוקתך as obedience to the husband. Ramban rejects that meaning and reads a longing for him despite the pain of pregnancy and childbirth.

sources.quote: תשוקתך. משמעתך, והטעם שתשמעי כל אשר יצוה עליך כי את ברשותו לעשות חפצו:
sources.says: Ibn Ezra explains תשוקתך as obeying the husband’s commands.

sources.quote: וְלֹא מָצָאתִי לְשׁוֹן תְּשׁוּקָה רַק בְּחֵשֶׁק וְתַאֲוָה. וְהַנָּכוֹן בְּעֵינַי שֶׁהֶעֱנִישׁ אוֹתָהּ שֶׁתִּהְיֶה נִכְסֶפֶת מְאֹד אֶל בַּעְלָהּ, וְלֹא תָּחוּשׁ לְצַעַר הַהֵרָיוֹן וְהַלֵּדָה,
sources.says: Ramban says תשוקה means desire and reads the verse as longing for the husband despite pregnancy and childbirth.

3:22.headline: The tree may promise a long life rather than immortality
3:22.body: Ibn Ezra says the tree of life would add many years to a person’s life. He reads לעולם here as a long duration, not endless life.

sources.quote: ועץ החיים. שיוסיף חיים ויחיה האדם שנים רבות ואין מלת לעולם עד עולם ועד, והנה כן "ועבדו לעולם" (שמות כא ו) "וישב שם עד עולם" (ש"א א כב), ורבים אחרים,
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the tree extends life for many years and that לעולם need not mean forever.

30:1.headline: Rachel's envy was of Leah's good deeds
30:1.body: Rashi, quoting the sages, says Rachel did not envy Leah's sons but her good deeds. She thought Leah must be more righteous, or she would not have children.

sources.quote: קִנְּאָה בְמַעֲשֶׂיהָ הַטּוֹבִים, אָמְרָה אִלּוּלֵי שֶׁצָּדְקָה מִמֶּנִּי לֹא זָכְתָה לְבָנִים
sources.says: Rashi says she envied her sister's good deeds, saying that unless Leah were more righteous than she, Leah would not have merited sons.

30:1.headline: 'Give me children' is heard as 'pray for me'
30:1.body: Rachel's words sound like a flat demand, and Rashi picks up on that: 'Is that how your father treated your mother? He prayed for her.' Ibn Ezra reads her request as asking Jacob to pray, as Isaac did.

sources.quote: וְכִי כָּךְ עָשָׂה אָבִיךָ לְאִמְּךָ? וְהֲלֹא הִתְפַּלֵּל עָלֶיהָ
sources.says: Rashi says: did your father do it this way for your mother? Did he not pray for her?

sources.quote: שתתפלל לשם כאשר עשה אביך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the request means that Jacob should pray to God, as his father did.

30:1.headline: מתה: 'I will die' or 'I am as good as dead'
30:1.body: Rashi says someone with no children is counted as dead, and Sforno compares Rachel to the dry tree in Isaiah. Rashbam says the stress here makes it a future word, 'I will die'.

sources.quote: מִכָּאן לְמִי שֶׁאֵין לוֹ בָנִים שֶׁחָשׁוּב כַּמֵּת
sources.says: Rashi says from here we learn that a person with no children is counted as dead.

sources.quote: כְּעִנְיַן "הֵן אֲנִי עֵץ יָבֵשׁ
sources.says: Sforno says it is like 'I am a dry tree'.

sources.quote: מתה אנכי - טעמו למטה שהוא פועל להבא
sources.says: Rashbam says that here the stress is on the lower syllable, which makes it a verb of the future.

30:3.headline: 'Bear on my knees' means 'she bears it for me'
30:3.body: Rashi quotes the Aramaic translation: 'I will raise him'. Radak says the child born on Rachel's knees would be raised by her, and counted as her own son.

sources.quote: כְּתַרְגּוּמוֹ וַאֲנָא אֱרַבֵּי
sources.says: Rashi says it is as the Aramaic translation has it, 'and I will raise'.

sources.quote: מַה שֶּׁתֵּלֵד יִהְיֶה עַל בִּרְכַּי וְאֶהְיֶה לוֹ לְאוֹמֶנֶת וְאֶחְשֹׁב שֶׁיִּהְיֶה בְּנִי
sources.says: Radak says what she bears will be on my knees, I will be his nurse, and I will count him as my son.

30:6.headline: דן comes from דנני, 'He judged me'
30:6.body: Rachel says God דנני, 'judged me', and so names the boy דן. Rashi says He judged her and found her in the right, and Radak says it was a verdict in her favor against her sister.

sources.quote: דָּנַנִּי וְחִיְּבַנִי וְזִכַּנִי
sources.says: Rashi says דנני means He judged me, found me liable, and then found me in the right.

sources.quote: שָׂמַנִי בְּדִינוֹ עִם אֲחוֹתִי וְרָאָה כִּי גַם אֲנִי רְאוּיָה לְבָנִים כָּמוֹהָ
sources.says: Radak says He set me in His judgment with my sister and saw that I too deserve children like her.

30:11.headline: בגד is written as one word, read as two: 'luck came'
30:11.body: Leah's cry is written בגד but read aloud as בא גד, 'luck has come'. Rashi gives that meaning and also 'betrayal', because Jacob went to her maid, and Bahya passes on a saying that Gad was born already circumcised.

sources.quote: בָּא מַזָּל טוֹב, כְּמוֹ גַּד גַּדִּי וְסָנוּק לָא
sources.says: Rashi says it means good luck has come.

sources.quote: דָּ"אַ לָמָּה נִקְרֵאת תֵּבָה אַחַת בָּגָד, כְּמוֹ בָּגַדְתָּ בִּי, כְּשֶׁבָּאתָ אֶל שִׁפְחָתִי
sources.says: Rashi says another reading is 'betrayal', as if she said you betrayed me when you came to my maid.

sources.quote: כָּתוּב מִלָּה אַחַת בְּלֹא אָלֶ״ף, וּפֵרוּשׁ בְּמַזָּל טוֹב בָּא זֶה, וּקְרִי שְׁתֵּי מִלּוֹת
sources.says: Radak says it is written as one word without an aleph, meaning he came with good luck, and is read as two words.

sources.quote: דָּרְשׁוּ רז״ל שֶׁנּוֹלַד מָהוּל
sources.says: Bahya says our sages taught that he was born circumcised.

30:18.headline: יששכר may hold two wages, or 'there is a wage'
30:18.body: Leah says God gave her שכרי, 'my wage'. Rashbam hears two wages in the double ש, one for the mandrakes and one for giving her maid to Jacob, and Radak reads the name as 'there is a wage'.

sources.quote: שני שכרים: אחד שכר הדודאים ואחד שכר שנתתי שפחתי לאישי
sources.says: Rashbam says two wages: one wage of the mandrakes and one wage for giving my maid to my husband.

sources.quote: קָרְאָה שֵׁם הַבֵּן הַזֶּה יִשָּׂשכָר, כְּלוֹמַר יֵשׁ שָׂכָר לִפְעֻלָּתִי
sources.says: Radak says she named this son יששכר, meaning there is a wage for my deed.

30:20.headline: זבדני is a verb found nowhere else in the Bible
30:20.body: Ibn Ezra says it means 'He gave me a portion' but notes there is no other verse with the word, and Ramban says no source for it can be found in the holy tongue. Rashbam says it means a good portion.

sources.quote: כטעם נתן לי חלק ואין לו אח במקרא
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it has the sense of 'gave me a portion', and has no sibling in Scripture.

sources.quote: לֹא מָצְאוּ לַמִּלָּה הַזֹּאת מוֹצָא בִּלְשׁוֹן הַקֹּדֶשׁ
sources.says: Ramban says they found no origin for this word in the holy tongue.

sources.quote: זבד - לשון חלק ומנה יפה לפי הענין
sources.says: Rashbam says זבד is a word for a portion, a fine share, as the matter requires.

30:20.headline: זבולון comes from a word for 'home'
30:20.body: Leah hopes that now her husband will live with her. Rashi links the verb to the house in 1 Kings, a home to dwell in, and adds that she now has sons to match all his wives.

sources.quote: בֵּית מָדוֹר, מֵעַתָּה לֹא תְהֵא עִקַּר דִּירָתוֹ אֶלָּא עִמִּי שֶׁיֵּשׁ לִי בָנִים כְּנֶגֶד כָּל נָשָׁיו
sources.says: Rashi says it means a dwelling place: from now his main home will be with me, since I have sons to match all his wives.

sources.quote: יזבול עמי יהיה זבולו עמי תמיד
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means he will dwell with me, his dwelling will always be with me.

sources.quote: כמו: בנה בניתי בית זבול לך. ל' דירה
sources.says: Rashbam says it is like 'I have built a house of dwelling for You', a word for a residence.

30:21.headline: דינה: Leah 'judged herself' and prayed for a girl
30:21.body: The verse does not say why she was named Dinah. Rashi says Leah judged herself: another boy would leave Rachel with fewer sons than the maids, so she prayed and the child became a girl.

sources.quote: פֵּרְשׁוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ שֶׁדָּנָה לֵאָה דִּין בְּעַצְמָהּ, אִם זֶה זָכָר לֹא תְהֵא רָחֵל אֲחוֹתִי כְּאַחַת הַשְּׁפָחוֹת, וְהִתְפַּלְּלָה עָלָיו וְנֶהְפַּךְ לִנְקֵבָה
sources.says: Rashi says our sages explained that Leah judged herself: if this is a boy, my sister Rachel will not be like one of the maids, and she prayed and it turned into a girl.

30:21.headline: No pregnancy is mentioned for Dinah, so she may be a twin
30:21.body: For every other child the verse says the mother conceived, but for Dinah it only says 'she bore a daughter'. Radak and Chizkuni say this hints that Dinah was born together with Zebulun.

sources.quote: נִרְאֶה כִּי דִּינָה תְּאוֹמָה הָיְתָה עִם זְבוּלוּן, לְפִיכָךְ אָמַר וְאַחַר יָלְדָה בַּת, וְלֹא אָמַר ״וַתֵּלֶד עוֹד
sources.says: Radak says it seems Dinah was a twin with Zebulun, which is why it says 'afterwards she bore a daughter', and not 'she bore again'.

sources.quote: אין כתיב בה הריון ללמדך שהיא היתה תאומים לזבולון
sources.says: Chizkuni says no pregnancy is written for her, to teach that she was a twin with Zebulun.

30:32.headline: חום means a dark sheep, and may come from 'heat'
30:32.body: Radak says it means black, and mentions a similar use in Arabic. Ibn Ezra says it may be named for heat, because black is hotter than white.

sources.quote: חוּם. שָׁחֹר. וְכֵן אָמַר בִּלְשׁוֹן עֲרָבִי בְּמִי שֶׁהוּא שָׁחֹר הָרֹאשׁ וְהַגָּרוֹן מִן הַצֹּאן, יֹאמְרוּ לוֹ חוּם
sources.says: Radak says חום means black, and in Arabic a sheep with a black head and throat is called חום.

sources.quote: ויתכן שנקרא השחרות כן מפני החום כי השחרות יותר חום מן הלבן
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says blackness may be called this because of the heat, since black is hotter than white.

30:38.headline: ברהטים are channels where the water runs
30:38.body: Rashi says they are the places where water runs, the pools made to water the flock. Radak backs it with the Aramaic translation of 'he ran', which is ורהט.

sources.quote: בִּמְרוּצוֹת הַמַּיִם, בַּבְּרֵכוֹת הָעֲשׂוּיוֹת בָּאָרֶץ לְהַשְׁקוֹת שָׁם הַצֹּאן
sources.says: Rashi says it means in the runs of the water, in the pools made in the ground to water the flock there.

sources.quote: תַּרְגּוּם ״וַיָּרָץ״ – ״וּרְהַט״, וּפֵרוּשׁ: מְקוֹם מְרוּצַת מַיִם
sources.says: Radak says the Aramaic for 'he ran' is ורהט, and so it means a place where water runs.

30:39.headline: עקדים are sheep marked at the ankles, from 'binding'
30:39.body: Rashi says the word names marks at the place where a sheep is tied up, the ankles, and Ibn Ezra also says a mark on the foot. Rashbam compares it to the word for tying Isaac's feet.

sources.quote: מְשֻׁנִּים בִּמְקוֹם עֲקִידָתָם, הֵם קַרְסֻלֵּי יְדֵיהֶם וְרַגְלֵיהֶם
sources.says: Rashi says it means those with marks in the place where they are bound, the ankles of their hands and feet.

sources.quote: ברגל והטעם שומה שעקדה הרגל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is in the foot, and means a mark that binds the foot.

sources.quote: עקוד ברגל, על שם: ויעקוד את יצחק קשירה ברגל
sources.says: Rashbam says עקוד means 'bound at the foot', after the verse where Abraham bound Isaac, a tying by the foot.

30:43.headline: 'He broke through': Jacob's wealth burst its fence
30:43.body: The verb פרץ means to break through, and Radak says it is as if Jacob's wealth broke down the fence because no place could hold it. Sforno says he broke the usual limit of success with flocks, and the sages say a breach opened for him like a taste of the world to come.

sources.quote: כְּאִלּוּ הָרְכוּשׁ פּוֹרֵץ הַגָּדֵר, כְּלוֹמַר שֶׁלֹּא יְכִילֶנּוּ מָקוֹם מֵרֻבּוֹ
sources.says: Radak says it is as if the wealth breaks the fence, that is, no place could hold it for how much there was.

sources.quote: פָּרַץ אֶת גְּבוּל הַהַצְלָחָה הַמֻּרְגֶּלֶת בִּמְלֶאכֶת מִרְעֵה הַצֹּאן
sources.says: Sforno says he broke through the usual limit of success in shepherding.

sources.quote: מְלַמֵּד שֶׁנִּפְרְצָה לוֹ פִּרְצָה מֵעֵין דֻּגְמָא שֶׁל עוֹלָם הַבָּא
sources.says: Bereshit Rabbah says it teaches that a breach opened for him like a sample of the world to come.

31:1.headline: עשה here means 'gathered', not 'made'
31:1.body: Laban's sons say Jacob 'made' all this wealth from their father's property. Rashi says עשה means to gather or acquire here, as in the verse where Saul 'made' an army.

sources.quote: עשה. כָּנַס, כְּמוֹ וַיַּעַשׂ חַיִל וַיַּךְ אֶת עֲמָלֵק
sources.says: Rashi says עשה means 'gathered', like 'he gathered an army and struck Amalek'.

31:13.headline: An angel says 'I am the God of Bethel'
31:13.body: In verse 11 it is an angel who speaks. Radak and Maimonides say an angel speaks in the name of the One who sent him, leaving out 'I am sent by', and Rashi adds only that the ה in האל is extra.

sources.quote: הַמַּלְאָךְ יְדַבֵּר בִּלְשׁוֹן אֲדֹנָיו כְּאִלּוּ הוּא מְדַבֵּר, כִּי יַעֲקֹב לֹא נָדַר לַמַּלְאָךְ אֶלָּא לָאֵל
sources.says: Radak says the angel speaks in the words of his master, as if he were speaking himself, because Jacob made his vow to God, not to an angel.

sources.quote: כאילו אמר: 'אנכי שלוח אלהי אביך', 'אנכי שלוח האל הנגלה עליך בבית אל
sources.says: Maimonides says it is as if the angel said: I am sent by the God of your father, I am sent by the God who appeared to you at Bethel.

sources.quote: כְּמוֹ אֵל בֵּית אֵל, הַהֵ"א יְתֵרָה
sources.says: Rashi says it means 'God of Bethel', with the ה extra.

31:13.headline: משחת: 'anointed' means to raise up and make holy
31:13.body: Jacob poured oil on the stone at Bethel. Rashi says the word is about greatness, as when a king is anointed, so the stone was raised to be an altar, and Rashbam says it means he set it apart as holy.

sources.quote: לְ' רִבּוּי וּגְדֻלָּה כְּשֶׁנִּמְשָׁח לַמַּלְכוּת, כָּךְ וַיִּצֹק שֶׁמֶן עַל רֹאשָׁהּ – לִהְיוֹת מְשׁוּחָה לְמִזְבֵּחַ
sources.says: Rashi says it is a word of increase and greatness, as when one is anointed to be king, so he poured oil on its head, to be anointed for the altar.

sources.quote: להקדישה ועדיין לא הקרבת עליה נדריך
sources.says: Rashbam says it was to make it holy, and you had not yet offered your vows on it.

31:15.headline: What is 'our money' that Laban ate?
31:15.body: Rachel and Leah say their father has eaten 'our money'. Rashi says he kept the pay for Jacob's labor, Chizkuni says the dowry he should have given them, and Rashbam says the profit he made from their marriage.

sources.quote: שֶׁעִכֵּב דְּמֵי שְׂכַר פְּעֻלָּתְךָ
sources.says: Rashi says he held back the pay for your work.

sources.quote: עכב לעצמו כסף נדוניתינו שהיה לו לתת לנו כדרך כל הארץ
sources.says: Chizkuni says he kept for himself our dowry money, which he should have given us as is the custom everywhere.

sources.quote: שנשתכר בנו בנשואינו, שהיה לך להשתכר ביגיע כפך לפרנסינו
sources.says: Rashbam says it is what he earned through our marriage, when he should have earned a living by his own labor to support us.

31:20.headline: Jacob 'stole Laban's heart': he stole his awareness
31:20.body: The verse says Jacob stole Laban's heart, and the commentators say he stole Laban's knowledge, since the heart is the seat of understanding. Laban uses the same words later, and Rashi says they mean 'you stole my mind'.

sources.quote: לא גנב יעקב כי אם דעתו, כי עיקר הדעת בלב
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says Jacob stole only his knowledge, because the main seat of knowledge is the heart.

sources.quote: גָּנַב דַּעְתּוֹ, כִּי הוּא הָיָה חוֹשֵׁב שֶׁיִּהְיֶה בָּעִיר וְהוּא הָלַךְ לוֹ
sources.says: Radak says he stole his mind, for Laban thought he would be in town, and he went away.

sources.quote: גָּנַבְתָּ אֶת דַּעְתִּי
sources.says: Rashi, on Laban's later words, says it means 'you stole my mind'.

31:26.headline: 'Captives of the sword': חרב can mean a whole army
31:26.body: Rashi says that any force that comes to war is called חרב, 'sword'. Radak says Laban means that Jacob led his daughters away like women captured by armed men, without anyone's knowledge.

sources.quote: כָּל חַיִל הַבָּא לַמִּלְחָמָה קָרוּי חֶרֶב
sources.says: Rashi says any army that comes to war is called 'sword'.

sources.quote: כְּנָשִׁים הַשְּׁבוּיוֹת בְּיַד בַּעֲלֵי חֶרֶב שֶׁיּוֹצְאוֹת מִמְּקוֹמָן שֶׁלֹּא מִדַּעַת
sources.says: Radak says it is like women taken captive by men of the sword, who leave their places without knowing.

31:29.headline: אל can mean 'God' or 'power': 'I have the power'
31:29.body: The phrase יש לאל ידי means 'it is within my power'. Rashi says the word אל, also a name of God, is named for strength and might, Ibn Ezra reads it as 'power', and Radak quotes the Aramaic word for strength.

sources.quote: יֵשׁ כֹּחַ וְחַיִל בְּיָדִי לַעֲשׂוֹת עִמָּכֶם רַע, וְכָל אֵל שֶׁהוּא לְ' קֹדֶש עַל שֵׁם עִזּוּז וְרֹב אוֹנִים הוּא
sources.says: Rashi says it means I have strength and power to do you harm, and every אל that is a holy word is named for might and great strength.

sources.quote: כח כמו "כגבור אין איל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means strength, as in 'like a man with no strength'.

sources.quote: כְּתַרְגּוּמוֹ: ״חֵילָא
sources.says: Radak says it is as the Aramaic translation has it: strength.

31:33.headline: 'Jacob's tent' means Rachel's tent
31:33.body: Laban first searches 'Jacob's tent', then Leah's, then the maids'. Rashi says Jacob's tent is Rachel's, because Jacob was always with her, and he notes that only Rachel is called 'Jacob's wife' in a later verse.

sources.quote: הוּא אֹהֶל רָחֵל, שֶׁהָיָה יַעֲקֹב תָּדִיר אֶצְלָהּ; וְכֵן הוּא אוֹמֵר בְּנֵי רָחֵל אֵשֶׁת יַעֲקֹב וּבְכֻלָּן לֹא נֶאֱמַר אֵשֶׁת יַעֲקֹב
sources.says: Rashi says it is Rachel's tent, since Jacob was constantly with her, and it says 'sons of Rachel, Jacob's wife', and for none of the others is it said 'Jacob's wife'.

31:38.headline: לא שכלו means the ewes did not miscarry
31:38.body: The root שכל usually means to lose a child, and Rashi says here it means the ewes did not drop their young early, as in Hosea. Rashbam says the cause could have been poor grazing or poor watching.

sources.quote: לֹא הִפִּילוּ עִבּוּרָם, כְּמוֹ רֶחֶם מַשְׁכִּיל
sources.says: Rashi says they did not lose their unborn young, like 'a womb that miscarries'.

sources.quote: מתוך חוסר מרעה ומתוך שמירה פחותה
sources.says: Rashbam says it means they did not miscarry from lack of pasture or from poor guarding.

31:39.headline: גנבתי means 'what was stolen from me', not 'I stole'
31:39.body: Jacob does not confess to stealing. Rashi and Rashbam read the word as a thing stolen from him, by day or night, that he paid back, and Rashbam notes the vowel decides the sense.

sources.quote: גְנוּבַת יוֹם אוֹ גְנוּבַת לַיְלָה, הַכֹּל שִׁלַּמְתִּי
sources.says: Rashi says whether stolen by day or by night, I paid for all of it.

sources.quote: אבל גְּנֻבָתִּי קמץ פתרונו גניבת שלי
sources.says: Rashbam says a גנבתי with a kamatz means 'my theft', that is, what was stolen from me.

31:42.headline: 'The Fear of Isaac' may be a name for God
31:42.body: Jacob says 'the Fear of Isaac' where he could have said 'God of Isaac'. Rashi says Jacob would not use God's name for Isaac while he was alive, Ibn Ezra reads it as Isaac's own fear of God, and Chizkuni reads it as the fear Laban had of Isaac.

sources.quote: לֹא רָצָה לוֹמַר אֱלֹהֵי יִצְחָק, שֶׁאֵין הַקָּבָּ"ה מְיַחֵד שְׁמוֹ עַל הַצַּדִּיקִים בְּחַיֵּיהֶם
sources.says: Rashi says he did not want to say 'God of Isaac', because God does not attach His name to the righteous in their lifetime.

sources.quote: יראת יצחק את השם היא הועילתני, כי זכות האב תועיל לבן
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says Isaac's fear of God helped me, since a father's merit helps a son.

sources.quote: לולי הפחד שפחדת מיצחק אבי שהוא עשיר ושר גדול
sources.says: Chizkuni says: were it not for the fear you had of my father Isaac, who is rich and a great prince.

sources.quote: בפחד אביו יצחק זה כינוי אלהות
sources.says: Chizkuni says, on the same phrase in verse 53, that 'the fear of his father Isaac' is a name for God.

31:47.headline: גלעד is 'a heap of witness'; Laban says it in Aramaic
31:47.body: Laban calls the heap יגר שהדותא and Jacob calls it גלעד. Rashi says they mean the same thing, 'a heap that is a witness', in two languages, and Radak says each man named it in his own language.

sources.quote: גלעד. גַּל עֵד
sources.says: Rashi says גלעד is גל עד, 'a heap, a witness'.

sources.quote: יגר שהדותא. תַּרְגּוּמוֹ שֶׁל גַּלְעֵד
sources.says: Rashi says יגר שהדותא is the Aramaic translation of גלעד.

sources.quote: כָּל אֶחָד קָרָא לוֹ שֵׁם בִּלְשׁוֹנוֹ, לָבָן בִּלְשׁוֹן אֲרָמִי
sources.says: Radak says each one called it by a name in his own language, Laban in Aramaic.

31:49.headline: המצפה is the 'lookout', and also 'may God watch'
31:49.body: The name is explained in the verse: 'may the LORD watch between us'. Radak says Jacob named it for the high place where it stood and also for that prayer, and Ibn Ezra says יצף means 'will see'.

sources.quote: לְפִי שֶׁהֵקִימָהּ בְּמָקוֹם גָּבוֹהַּ, וְקָרָא אוֹתָהּ גַּם כֵּן מִצְפָּה לְעִנְיַן שֶׁאָמַר יִצֶף ה׳ בֵּינִי וּבֵינֶךָ
sources.says: Radak says because he set it up in a high place, and he also called it Mizpah because of what he said, 'may the LORD watch between me and you'.

sources.quote: וטעם יצף ד'. כמו ד' יראה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the sense of 'may the LORD watch' is like 'the LORD will see'.

31:51.headline: יריתי means 'I threw', and also 'I set up'
31:51.body: Laban says he 'threw' the pillar between them. Rashi says it is the verb for shooting an arrow, and Rashbam says it means 'I raised', since Jacob set it up on Laban's advice.

sources.quote: כְּמוֹ יָרָה בַיָּם, כְּזֶה שֶׁהוּא יוֹרֶה הַחֵץ
sources.says: Rashi says it is like 'he threw into the sea', like one who shoots an arrow.

sources.quote: זקפתי, יעקב ירה אותה בעצת לבן
sources.says: Rashbam says it means 'I raised up', and that Jacob set it up on Laban's advice.

31:52.headline: אם here means 'that', not 'if'
31:52.body: Laban says 'I will not pass this heap to you'. Rashi and Radak say the word אם works like אשר, 'that', so this is a pledge about what Laban will do, not 'if'.

sources.quote: הֲרֵי אִם מְשַׁמֵּשׁ בִּלְשׁוֹן אֲשֶׁר, כְּמוֹ עַד אִם דִּבַּרְתִּי דְּבָרָי
sources.says: Rashi says אם is used in the sense of אשר, like 'until I have spoken my words'.

sources.quote: טַעְמוֹ בִּמְקוֹם שִׁי״ן הַשִּׁמּוּשׁ, כְּאִלּוּ אָמַר שֶׁאֲנִי שֶׁאַתָּה
sources.says: Radak says it stands in the place of the ש that joins, as if he had said 'that I' and 'that you'.

31:54.headline: לחם here means a whole meal, not just 'bread'
31:54.body: Jacob invites everyone to eat לחם. Rashi says any kind of food is called לחם, and that Jacob slaughtered animals for a feast.

sources.quote: כָּל דְּבַר מַאֲכָל קָרוּי לֶחֶם, כְּמוֹ עֲבַד לְחֶם רַב
sources.says: Rashi says any food is called לחם, like 'he made a great feast'.

sources.quote: שָׁחַט בְּהֵמוֹת לְמִשְׁתֶּה
sources.says: Rashi says he slaughtered animals for a feast.

32:4.headline: Were Jacob's "messengers" real angels? Rashi says yes
32:4.body: מלאכים means both angels and human messengers. Rashi, quoting Bereshit Rabbah, says these were real angels, while Ibn Ezra says they were Jacob's servants, and Maimonides cites this verse as an example of a human messenger.

sources.quote: מַלְאָכִים מַמָּש
sources.says: Rashi says these were real angels.

sources.quote: ואלה המלאכים הם מעבדיו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says these messengers were some of his servants.

sources.ref: Guide for the Perplexed, Part 2, Chapter 6:2
sources.quote: מלאך" נאמר א) על שליח מבני האדם: "וַיִּשְׁלַח יַעֲקֹב מַלְאָכִים
sources.says: Maimonides says מלאך is said of a human messenger, and gives "Jacob sent messengers" as the example.

32:5.headline: גרתי adds up to 613, the number of commandments
32:5.body: Rashi says Jacob's "I lived with Laban" (גרתי) has the letter-value 613. He is telling Esau that he kept all the commandments while living with Laban.

sources.quote: גַּרְתִּי בְּגִימַטְרִיָּא תרי"ג, כְּלוֹמַר, עִם לָבָן גַּרְתִּי וְתַרְיַ"ג מִצְוֹת שָׁמַרְתִּי וְלֹא לָמַדְתִּי מִמַּעֲשָׂיו הָרָעִים
sources.says: Rashi says גרתי adds up to 613, meaning Jacob lived with Laban and kept the 613 commandments and did not learn from his wicked deeds.

32:8.headline: Two kinds of fear: of being killed, and of having to kill
32:8.body: The verse says Jacob "feared" and "was distressed". Rashi says the first is fear of being killed and the second is distress at the thought of killing others.

sources.quote: וַיִּירָא שֶׁמָּא יֵהָרֵג, וַיֵּצֶר לוֹ אִם יַהֲרֹג הוּא אֶת אֲחֵרִים
sources.says: Rashi says "he feared" that he might be killed, and "he was distressed" at the thought that he himself might kill others.

32:13.headline: Jacob's "surely good" splits into his merit and his fathers'
32:13.body: God said "I will surely do good with you". Rashi, quoting Bereshit Rabbah, reads the doubled verb as two promises: one for Jacob's own merit, one for his fathers' merit.

sources.quote: הֵיטֵב בִּזְכוּתְךָ, אֵיטִיב בִּזְכוּת אֲבוֹתֶיך
sources.says: Rashi says "do good" is for your merit and "I will do good" is for your fathers' merit.

32:17.headline: "Space" between the herds was meant to astonish Esau
32:17.body: Jacob tells his servants to leave a gap (רוח) between the herds. Rashi says it let Esau's eye take in each herd and marvel at the size of the gift, while Ibn Ezra says the word means a pause, as with relief between blows.

sources.quote: עֵדֶר לִפְנֵי חֲבֵרוֹ מְלֹא עַיִן, כְּדֵי לְהַשְׂבִּיעַ עֵינוֹ שֶׁל אוֹתוֹ רָשָׁע וּלְתַוֵּהוּ עַל רִבּוּי הַדּוֹרוֹן
sources.says: Rashi says each herd should be an eyeful before the next, to satisfy the wicked one's eye and amaze him at the size of the gift.

sources.quote: הפרש, וקרוב ממנו "כי היתה הרוחה" (שמות ח יא), הפרשה בין מכה למכה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word means a gap, close to "there was relief", the break between one plague and the next.

32:21.headline: "Face" also means anger, as in "wipe away his face"
32:21.body: Ibn Ezra says פניו here means his anger. Maimonides lists "anger" among the meanings of פנים, and cites "her face was no longer hers".

sources.quote: ופניו כעסו וכן "ופניה לא הי' לה עוד
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says his face means his anger, as in "her face was no longer hers".

sources.ref: Guide for the Perplexed, Part 1, Chapter 37:2
sources.quote: הוא שמו של הכעס: "וּפָנֶיהָ לֹא הָיוּ לָהּ עוֹד
sources.says: Maimonides says פנים is also the name of anger, and cites "her face was no longer hers".

32:25.headline: "Left alone" means Jacob went back for small jars
32:25.body: Rashi says the word "left" hints that Jacob had forgotten small jars and went back for them. Rashbam gives a plain reading: Jacob stayed behind alone, meaning to slip away by another road.

sources.quote: שָׁכַח פַּכִּים קְטַנִּים וְחָזַר עֲלֵיהֶם
sources.says: Rashi says he forgot small jars and went back for them.

sources.quote: ורצה לעבור אחריהם, כדי לברוח דרך אחרת שלא יפגשנו עשו
sources.says: Rashbam says Jacob wanted to cross after them and flee by another way so Esau would not meet him.

32:25.headline: "Wrestled" may come from dust, or from a hug and a tie
32:25.body: Ibn Ezra and Radak link ויאבק to אבק, "dust", raised by their feet. Rashi says it is an Aramaic word for binding, as wrestlers grip and embrace each other.

sources.quote: וְלִי נִרְאֶה שֶׁהוּא לְשׁוֹן וַיִּתְקַשֵּׁר, וְלָשׁוֹן אֲרַמִּי הוּא, בָּתַר דַּאֲבִיקוּ בֵיהּ, וַאֲבֵיק לֵיהּ מֵיבַק – לְשׁוֹן עֲנִיבָה, שֶׁכֵּן דֶּרֶךְ שְׁנַיִם שֶׁמִּתְעַצְּמִים לְהַפִּיל אִישׁ אֶת רֵעֵהוּ, שֶׁחוֹבְקוֹ וְאוֹבְקוֹ בִּזְרוֹעוֹתָיו
sources.says: Rashi says it is an Aramaic word meaning "tie", since wrestlers hug and grip each other in their arms.

sources.quote: מגזרת אבק, עד שעלה אבק ביניהם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it comes from "dust", until dust rose between them.

sources.quote: נִתְאַבֵּק עִמּוֹ עַד שֶׁהֶעֱלוּ אָבָק
sources.says: Radak says he wrestled with him until they raised dust.

32:25.headline: The "man" who wrestled Jacob is an angel, say the commentators
32:25.body: איש means "man", but Radak says here it is an angel who looks like a man, and Maimonides says the whole scene was a vision. Rashi adds that the sages said he was Esau's guardian angel.

sources.quote: מַלְאָךְ, וְכֵן ״וְהִנֵּה אִישׁ עֹמֵד לְנֶגְדּו
sources.says: Radak says איש here means an angel, as in "behold, a man standing opposite him".

sources.quote: וּפֵרְשׁוּ רַזִ"לִ שֶׁהוּא שָׂרוֹ שֶׁל עֵשָׂו
sources.says: Rashi says the sages explained that he was Esau's guardian angel.

sources.ref: Guide for the Perplexed, Part 2, Chapter 42:3
sources.quote: וכן אני אומר גם בפרשת יעקב על דבריו "וַיֵּאָבֵק אִישׁ עִמּוֹ" (בראשית לב,כה), שזה בצורת התגלות, כיוון שהתברר לבסוף שהוא מלאך
sources.says: Maimonides says the wrestling was a revealed vision, since it became clear in the end that he was an angel.

32:26.headline: "Pulled loose": a word that can also mean "pitch a tent"
32:26.body: Rashi says the hip socket was pulled out of its joint, and compares "lest my soul be torn from you". Chizkuni says some words flip between building and tearing down, and gives this one: it can mean to tear out, or to pitch a tent.

sources.quote: נִתְקַעְקְעָה מִמְּקוֹם מַחְבַּרְתָּהּ, וְדוֹמֶה לוֹ פֶּן תֵּקַע נַפְשִׁי מִמֵּךְ (ירמיהו ו'), לְשׁוֹן הֲסָרָה
sources.says: Rashi says it was pulled out from its joint, like "lest my soul be torn from you", a word of removal.

sources.quote: יש דברים ובפתרונם מתהפכים לשתי מליצות בנין וסתירה כגון זה. וכגון פן תקע נפשי ממך ומצינו ויעקב תקע את אהלו בהר
sources.says: Chizkuni says some words can mean both building and destroying, and gives this word, comparing "pitch his tent on the mountain".

32:29.headline: The name Israel is explained as "you strove" or "you became great"
32:29.body: The verse explains the name with כי שרית. Onkelos translates it as "you became great before the Lord", Rashbam derives it from "in his strength he strove with God", and Chizkuni says Jacob became equal to angels in authority but not over them.

sources.quote: אֲרֵי רַבְרְבַת קֳדָם יְי
sources.says: Onkelos says "for you have become great before the Lord".

sources.quote: מגזרת באונו שרה את אלהים כמו קנה קנית. עשה עשית
sources.says: Rashbam says שרית comes from "in his strength he strove with God", a past form like קנה קנית.

sources.quote: נעשית שווה למלאכים בשררה וממשלה אבל לא עליהם
sources.says: Chizkuni says Jacob became equal to angels in authority and rule, but not over them.

32:30.headline: The angel will not give his name: it changes with each mission
32:30.body: Jacob asks the angel's name. Rashi, quoting Bereshit Rabbah, says angels have no fixed name because it changes with each mission, and Ramban says knowing it would not help Jacob, since all power belongs to God alone.

sources.quote: אֵין לָנוּ שֵׁם קָבוּעַ, מִשְׁתַּנִּים שְׁמוֹתֵנוּ, הַכֹּל לְפִי מִצְוַת עֲבוֹדַת הַשְּׁלִיחוּת שֶׁאָנוּ מִשְׁתַּלְּחִים
sources.says: Rashi says angels have no fixed name; their names change according to the mission they are sent on.

sources.quote: אֵין לְךָ בִּידִיעַת שְׁמִי תּוֹעֶלֶת, כִּי אֵין הַכֹּחַ וְהַיְּכֹלֶת בִּלְתִּי לַה' לְבַדּו
sources.says: Ramban says knowing the angel's name would not help Jacob, since power belongs only to God.

32:33.headline: The "thigh sinew" is named for jumping out of place
32:33.body: Rashi says the sinew is called הנשה because it leaped (נשה) from its place and went up. Radak says the same: it was torn loose and rose onto the socket.

sources.quote: לְפִי שֶׁנָּשָׁה מִמְּקוֹמוֹ וְעָלָה, וְהוּא לְשׁוֹן קְפִיצָה
sources.says: Rashi says it is named this because it leaped from its place and went up, a word of jumping.

sources.quote: נִקְרָא כֵּן לְפִי שֶׁנָּשָׁה מִמְּקוֹמוֹ וְעָלָה (חולין צא), כְּלוֹמַר נִפְסַק וְנֶעֱלָה עַל הַכַּף שֶׁהוּא דָּבֵק בּו
sources.says: Radak says it is called this because it moved from its place and rose, torn loose and lifted onto the socket it clung to.

33:2.headline: Jacob put the ones he loved most at the back
33:2.body: Jacob lines up the maids first, then Leah, then Rachel and Joseph last. Rashi says the last is the dearest, and Radak adds that Esau might calm down after attacking the first in line.

sources.quote: אַחֲרוֹן אַחֲרוֹן חָבִיב
sources.says: Rashi says the last one is the dearest.

sources.quote: אַחֲרוֹן אַחֲרוֹן חָבִיב, אוּלַי יָנוּחַ כַּעֲסוֹ בַּהֲרִיגַת הָרִאשׁוֹנִים וְיַנִּיחַ הָאַחֲרוֹנִים
sources.says: Radak says the last is the dearest, since perhaps his anger would settle after killing the first ones and he would leave the last.

33:4.headline: Dots over 'and he kissed him': a real kiss or a bite?
33:4.body: In the Torah scroll this word has dots above it, and the sages argue what they mean. One says Esau's heart softened and he kissed him fully, another that he meant to bite him but Jacob's neck turned to marble, and Ibn Ezra says the plain sense is a real kiss, since both wept.

sources.quote: אָמַר רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַאי, הֲלָכָה הִיא בְּיָדוּעַ שֶׁעֵשָׂו שׂוֹנֵא לְיַעֲקֹב, אֶלָּא שֶׁנִּכְמְרוּ רַחֲמָיו בְּאוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה וּנְשָׁקוֹ בְּכָל לִבּוֹ
sources.says: Rashi quotes Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai: it is a known rule that Esau hates Jacob, but at that moment his compassion was stirred and he kissed him with all his heart.

sources.quote: מְלַמֵּד שֶׁלֹא בָּא לְנַשְּׁקוֹ אֶלָּא לְנָשְׁכוֹ, וְנַעֲשָׂה צַוָּארוֹ שֶׁל אָבִינוּ יַעֲקֹב שֶׁל שַׁיִשׁ וְקָהוּ שִׁנָּיו שֶׁל אוֹתוֹ רָשָׁע
sources.says: Bereshit Rabbah says it teaches he came to bite and not to kiss, so our father Jacob's neck became marble and the wicked man's teeth were dulled.

sources.quote: שֶׁנְּשִׁיקָה זוֹ לֹא הָיְתָה בְּכָל לִבּוֹ רַק נְשִׁיקַת אַף
sources.says: Bahya says the dots teach that this kiss was not with all his heart, but a kiss of anger.

sources.quote: על דרך הפשט לא חשב עשו לעשות רע לאחיו והעד ויבכו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says on the plain sense Esau did not plan to harm his brother, and the proof is that they wept.

33:7.headline: Joseph stepped in front of his mother to hide her from Esau
33:7.body: For the others, the mothers come forward before their children, but for Rachel Joseph comes first. Rashi says he stood in front of her so Esau would not stare at her beauty, while Rashbam gives the plain reason: the man is usually named first.

sources.quote: בְּכֻלָּן הָאִמָּהוֹת נִגָּשׁוֹת לִפְנֵי הַבָּנִים, אֲבָל בְּרָחֵל יוֹסֵף נִגַּשׁ לְפָנֶיהָ, אָמַר אִמִּי יְפַת תֹּאַר, שֶׁמָּא יִתְלֶה בָהּ עֵינָיו אוֹתוֹ רָשָׁע, אֶעֱמֹד כְּנֶגְדָהּ וַאֲעַכְּבֶנּוּ מִלְּהִסְתַּכֵּל בָּהּ
sources.says: Rashi says that for all the others the mothers came before their sons, but with Rachel Joseph came before her, thinking: my mother is beautiful, perhaps that wicked man will set his eyes on her, so I will stand before her.

sources.quote: לפי הפשט: דרך להזכיר את האיש תחילה
sources.says: Rashbam says that on the plain sense it is the custom to name the man first.

33:10.headline: 'Like seeing the face of אלהים': God, an angel, or a prince?
33:10.body: Ibn Ezra reads אלהים as an angel, and Sforno as the custom of visiting a ruler. The sages in Bahya say Jacob chose words that can be heard two ways: flattering to Esau, but also, in another sense, not praise at all.

sources.quote: כראות פני אלהים. מלאך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says 'like seeing the face of God' means an angel.

sources.quote: כְּמִנְהָג בִּפְקוֹד אֶת הַשָּׂרִים, כְּאָמְרוֹ "וְלֹא יֵרָאוּ פָנַי רֵיקָם
sources.says: Sforno says it is like the custom of visiting princes, as it says 'they shall not appear empty-handed'.

sources.quote: לְפִי שֶׁהוּא לָשׁוֹן כּוֹלֵל שְׁנֵי מַשְׁמָעוּיוֹת, לִשְׁבַח וְלִגְנַאי
sources.says: Bahya says it is permitted because the wording includes two meanings, one of praise and one of contempt.

sources.quote: וְכֵן ״אֱלֹהִים״ לְשׁוֹן עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה
sources.says: Bahya adds that אלהים can also be a word for idols.

33:11.headline: 'Take my blessing' means 'take my gift'
33:11.body: Jacob offers his 'blessing', and Rashi and Radak say here it means the gift he sent. Rashi adds that a ברכה given on a visit is a word of greeting and peace.

sources.quote: מִנְחָתִי, מִנְחָה זוֹ הַבָּאָה עַל רְאִיַּת פָּנִים וְלִפְרָקִים אֵינָה בָאָה אֶלָּא לִשְׁאֵלַת שָׁלוֹם
sources.says: Rashi says it means my gift, a gift that comes on seeing someone's face, and sometimes comes only to ask after his peace.

sources.quote: מִנְחָתִי, כְּמוֹ ״קַח־נָא בְרָכָה מֵאֵת עַבְדֶּךָ
sources.says: Radak says it means my gift, like 'please take a blessing from your servant'.

33:13.headline: עלות here means 'nursing', not 'going up'
33:13.body: Jacob says the sheep and cattle are עלות. Rashi links the word to עולל, a nursing child, and Radak says they are nursing and their young are infants, while Ibn Ezra ties it to a verse in Isaiah.

sources.quote: מְגַדְּלוֹת עוֹלְלֵיהֶן, לְשׁוֹן עוֹלֵל וְיוֹנֵק
sources.says: Rashi says it means raising their young, from the word for a child and a nursing infant.

sources.quote: שֶׁהֵם מֵינִיקוֹת וּבְנֵיהֶם הֵם עוֹלְלֵי יָמִים
sources.says: Radak says it means they are nursing and their young are infants.

sources.quote: עלות. כמו עלות ינהל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is like the word in 'He will gently lead the nursing ewes'.

33:14.headline: לרגל means 'for the sake of', or 'at the pace of feet'
33:14.body: Maimonides says רגל can mean a cause, and gives this verse as a common example: 'because of the work ahead of me'. Ibn Ezra offers both readings: 'because of', or simply the feet of the herds.

sources.quote: כי דבר שהוא בגלל דבר־מה, הרי אותו דבר־מה הוא סיבה לדבר. זהו שימוש נפוץ
sources.says: Maimonides says רגל can mean a cause, since a thing that is because of something has that something as its cause, and this is a common use.

sources.quote: לְרֶגֶל הַמְּלָאכָה אֲשֶׁר לְפָנַי וּלְרֶגֶל הַיְלָדִים
sources.says: Maimonides cites 'for the work before me and for the children' as an example.

sources.quote: ויתכן להיות לרגל כמשמעו שהוליכם על רגליהם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it may also be taken literally, that he led them on their feet.

33:18.headline: שלם can be 'whole', 'safe', or the name of a city
33:18.body: Rashi says Jacob arrived whole in three ways: in his body, healed of his limp; in his money, with nothing missing; and in his Torah. Ibn Ezra says it just means he arrived safe, and Rashbam says it is a city named Shalem.

sources.quote: שָׁלֵם בְּגוּפוֹ, שֶׁנִּתְרַפֵּא מִצָּלַעְתּוֹ; שָׁלֵם בְּמָמוֹנוֹ, שֶׁלֹּא חָסַר כְּלוּם מִכָּל אוֹתוֹ דּוֹרוֹן; שָׁלֵם בְּתוֹרָתוֹ, שֶׁלֹּא שָׁכַח תַּלְמוּדוֹ בְּבֵית לָבָן
sources.says: Rashi says whole in his body, as he was healed of his limp; whole in his money, as nothing was lost from that gift; whole in his Torah, as he did not forget his learning in Laban's house.

sources.quote: שם התואר והטעם שבא בשלום שלא אירע לו שום מאורע
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is a describing word, meaning he came in peace and nothing happened to him.

sources.quote: אל עיר ששמה שלם. כמו: ותבאנה בית לחם
sources.says: Rashbam says it means to a city called Shalem, like 'and they came to Bethlehem'.

33:19.headline: קשיטה is a coin, and Rabbi Akiva knew it from abroad
33:19.body: Rashi says Rabbi Akiva heard people in the sea-cities call a certain coin a קשיטה, and Rashbam says it was a kind of coin with that name. Radak says Onkelos read it as lambs.

sources.quote: מָעָה. אָרַ"עֲ כְּשֶׁהָלַכְתִּי לִכְרַכֵּי הַיָּם הָיוּ קוֹרִין לְמָעָה קְשִׂיטָה
sources.says: Rashi says it is a small coin; Rabbi Akiva said that when he went to the sea-cities they called a small coin a קשיטה.

sources.quote: מין מטבע ששמה כן
sources.says: Rashbam says it is a kind of coin whose name is that.

sources.quote: וְדַעַת אוּנְקְלוֹס כְּבָשׂוֹת
sources.says: Radak says Onkelos takes it to mean lambs.

34:1.headline: She went out 'to see' and was seen
34:1.body: The verse says Dinah went out to see the daughters of the land, and the midrash plays on the word: she went out to see, and she was seen. Radak gives the plain sense, that she left her parents' tent outside the city and went into the town.

sources.quote: וּבַמִּדְרָשׁ ״לִרְאוֹת״, יָצְאָה לִרְאוֹת וְנִרְאֵית
sources.says: Bahya quotes the midrash on 'to see': she went out to see and was seen.

sources.quote: וּבָאָה אֶל הָעִיר לִרְאוֹת בִּבְנוֹת הָאָרֶץ
sources.says: Radak says she came into the city to see the daughters of the land.

34:12.headline: מהר is the marriage payment, and ומתן the gifts
34:12.body: Ramban says מהר is the sum set aside for a bride, the 'ketubah', as in the verse on 'the מהר of virgins'. The next word, מתן, means presents to her father and brothers.

sources.quote: מֹהַר, כְּתֻבָּה, שֶׁהוּא הַדָּבָר הַנִּתָּן לִבְתוּלָה
sources.says: Ramban says מהר is a marriage deed, the thing given to a virgin.

sources.quote: וּמַתָּן, מִגְדָּנוֹת אוֹ כֶּסֶף וְזָהָב לְאָבִיהָ וּלְאַחֶיהָ
sources.says: Ramban says מתן means gifts, or silver and gold, for her father and brothers.

34:13.headline: במרמה: 'with deceit', or just 'with cleverness'?
34:13.body: Rashi first reads it as 'with wisdom', then, quoting the midrash, says the verse is telling us there was no deceit, since Shechem had defiled Dinah. Chizkuni says the trick was in asking everyone to be circumcised.

sources.quote: במרמה. בְּחָכְמָה
sources.says: Rashi says במרמה means 'with wisdom'.

sources.quote: הַכָּתוּב אוֹמֵר שֶׁלֹּא הָיְתָה רְמִיָּה, שֶׁהֲרֵי טִמֵּא אֶת דִּינָה אֲחֹתָם
sources.says: Rashi says Scripture is saying it was not deceit, since he had defiled their sister Dinah.

sources.quote: במרמה ששאלו להמול כל זכר וסבורים בני יעקב שלא יאותו להמול רק שכם וחמור בשביל אהבת הנערה
sources.says: Chizkuni says the deceit was that they asked every male to be circumcised, thinking only Shechem and Hamor would agree, for love of the girl.

34:15.headline: נאות means 'we will agree', and is related to 'fitting'
34:15.body: Rashi says נאות means 'we will consent', linking it to a verb in Kings. Ibn Ezra, on the same word in verse 22, links the root to a word for 'it is fitting'.

sources.quote: נאות לכם. נִתְרַצֶּה לָכֶם, לְשׁוֹן וַיֵּאֹתוּ
sources.says: Rashi says it means 'we will consent to you', a word like 'they agreed'.

sources.quote: יאותו. מגזרת "כי לך יאתה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it comes from the same root as 'it is fitting for You'.

34:21.headline: 'The land is wide of hands': spacious, or generous?
34:21.body: Rashi takes the phrase as a person whose hand is wide and generous, so do not lose the profit: there is merchandise here with no buyers. Ibn Ezra and Radak say it means the land has wide open spaces.

sources.quote: כְּאָדָם שֶׁיָּדוֹ רְחָבָה וּוַתְרָנִית; כְּלוֹמַר, אַל תַּפְסִידוּ כְּלוּם
sources.says: Rashi says it is like a person whose hand is open and generous, meaning: do not lose out at all.

sources.quote: רחבת ידים. מקומות כמו "ויד תהיה לך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means places, like 'you shall have a place' (literally, a hand).

sources.quote: הָאָרֶץ רַחֲבַת מְקוֹמוֹת הִיא וְיֵשׁ לָנוּ וְלָהֶם דַּי לִמְקוֹם מִרְעֶה
sources.says: Radak says the land has wide places, and there is enough pasture for us and for them.

34:25.headline: ויבאו על העיר בטח: who was 'secure'?
34:25.body: Rashi gives two readings: the men were in pain, or the brothers felt safe in their father's strength. Rashbam says the townspeople were sitting at ease and not on guard, and Radak says it means they came as if they were many.

sources.quote: שֶׁהָיוּ כוֹאֲבִים וּמִ"אַ בְּטוּחִים הָיוּ עַל כֹּחוֹ שֶׁל זָקֵן
sources.says: Rashi says they were in pain, and another view says they were confident in the strength of the old man.

sources.quote: שהיו יושבים בטח ולא נזהרו מהם
sources.says: Rashbam says they were sitting securely and were not on guard against them.

sources.quote: בֶּטַח. כְּאִלּוּ הָיוּ רַבִּים
sources.says: Radak says it means as if they were many.

34:29.headline: חילם here means 'their wealth', not 'their army'
34:29.body: The word חיל usually means an army or strength, but Rashi says here it means their money, as in 'my hand has made me this wealth'. Radak lists silver, gold and jewels.

sources.quote: מָמוֹנָם וְכֵן עָשָׂה לִי אֶת הַחַיִל הַזֶּה
sources.says: Rashi says it means their wealth, as in 'he has made me this wealth'.

sources.quote: כֶּסֶף וְזָהָב וּמַרְגָּלִיּוֹת
sources.says: Radak says it means silver, gold and pearls.

34:31.headline: הכזונה: 'like a harlot' or 'like ownerless property'?
34:31.body: The brothers ask whether their sister should be treated like a זונה. Rashi says it means something ownerless, which anyone may take, while Radak and Sforno say Shechem treated her like a prostitute and her insult must still be answered.

sources.quote: הכזונה. הֶפְקֵר
sources.says: Rashi says הכזונה means something ownerless.

sources.quote: יַעֲשֶׂה שְׁכֶם אֶת־אֲחוֹתֵנוּ, כְּאִשָּׁה זוֹנָה, וְלֹא נִקַּח נִקְמָתֵנוּ מִמֶּנּוּ
sources.says: Radak says: should Shechem treat our sister like a harlot, and we not take our revenge on him?

sources.quote: שֶׁאֵינָהּ זוֹנָה וְרָאוּי לִתְבֹּעַ עֶלְבּוֹנָהּ, וְשֶׁהִיא אָחוֹת לָנוּ וְרָאוּי לָנוּ לִתְבֹּעַ עֶלְבּוֹנָהּ
sources.says: Sforno says she is not a harlot and her insult should be claimed, and she is our sister and it is right for us to claim it.

35:1.headline: ושב שם: does it mean 'live there' or 'settle your mind'?
35:1.body: God tells Jacob to go up to Bethel and ושב there, and Ramban admits he does not know what 'dwell there' adds. Sforno and Bahya read it as steadying the mind first, before building the altar.

sources.quote: לֹא יָדַעְתִּי מַהוּ "וְשֶׁב שָׁם
sources.says: Ramban says he does not know what 'dwell there' means.

sources.quote: וְשֶׁב שָׁם. לְכַוֵּן דַּעְתְּךָ קֹדֶם שֶׁתִּבְנֶה הַמִּזְבֵּחַ
sources.says: Sforno says 'dwell there' means to focus your mind before you build the altar.

sources.quote: טַעֲמוֹ שֶׁיִּתְיַשֵּׁב שִׂכְלוֹ שָׁם
sources.says: Bahya says it means that his mind would settle there.

35:4.headline: Why Jacob buried the idols, when the law says to scatter them
35:4.body: Ramban says idols are not buried: they must be ground up and scattered or thrown into the sea. His answer, followed by Bahya and Sforno, is that these idols had already been canceled, so burying them was enough.

sources.quote: עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה וּמְשַׁמְּשֶׁיהָ אֵינָן מִן הַנִּקְבָּרִים, אֲבָל צָרִיךְ שֶׁיְּהֵא מְפָרֵר וְזוֹרֶה לָרוּחַ אוֹ מַטִּיל לַיָּם
sources.says: Ramban says idols and their fittings are not among things that are buried, but must be ground up and scattered to the wind or thrown into the sea.

sources.quote: אֲבָל זֶה יוֹרֶה כִּי מֻתֶּרֶת הָיְתָה, וְכֵיוָן שֶׁנִּתְבַּטְּלָה הֻתְּרָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַרְנוּ, וּלְפִיכָךְ דַּי בִּקְבוּרָה
sources.says: Bahya says this shows they were permitted, and once they were canceled, as we said, burial was enough.

sources.quote: וְלֹא אִבְּדָם מִפְּנֵי שֶׁהָיוּ כְּבָר מְבֻטָּלִים וּמֻתָּרִין בַּהֲנָאָה
sources.says: Sforno says he did not destroy them because they had already been canceled and were permitted for use.

35:6.headline: לוז, 'almond tree': whoever enters it turns fresh with good deeds
35:6.body: The verse says Jacob came to Luz 'in the land of Canaan', which Radak says tells us there is another Luz. Bereshit Rabbah plays on the name, also an almond tree: whoever enters it becomes moist with good deeds like a luz.

sources.quote: מְלַמֵּד שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוּז אַחֵר
sources.says: Radak says this teaches that there is another Luz.

sources.quote: שֶׁכָּל מִי שֶׁנִּכְנַס לְתוֹכָהּ הִרְטִיב מִצְווֹת וּמַעֲשִׂים טוֹבִים כַּלּוּז
sources.says: Bereshit Rabbah says that everyone who enters it becomes moist with commandments and good deeds, like a luz.

35:8.headline: What is Rebecca's nurse doing in Jacob's story?
35:8.body: The verse suddenly mentions the death of Deborah, Rebecca's nurse, and Rashi asks what she was doing in Jacob's house. His answer is that Rebecca had promised to send for Jacob, so Deborah went to fetch him and died on the way back.

sources.quote: מָה עִנְיַן דְּבוֹרָה בְּבֵית יַעֲקֹב? אֶלָּא לְפִי שֶׁאָמְרָה רִבְקָה לְיַעֲקֹב וְשָׁלַחְתִּי וּלְקַחְתִּיךָ מִשָּׁם, שָׁלְחָה דְבוֹרָה אֶצְלוֹ לְפַדַּן אֲרָם לָצֵאת מִשָּׁם, וּמֵתָה בַדֶּרֶךְ
sources.says: Rashi asks what Deborah has to do with Jacob's house, and answers that Rebecca had said she would send for him, so she sent Deborah to Paddan Aram, and she died on the way.

35:8.headline: אלון בכות: 'oak of weeping', and a Greek pun
35:8.body: The verse says Jacob named the place 'oak of weeping'. Radak quotes a midrash that plays on Greek, where אלון means 'another', since news came that his mother had died while Jacob mourned Deborah, and Rashbam says Scripture lists every stop of the return.

sources.quote: לָשׁוֹן יְוָנִית הוּא, אַלּוֹן – אֶחָד, עַד שֶׁהוּא מְשַׁמֵּר אֶבְלוּת שֶׁל דְּבוֹרָה בָּאָה לוֹ בְּשׂוֹרָתָהּ שֶׁל אִמּוֹ שֶׁמֵּתָה
sources.says: Radak quotes Bereshit Rabbah: it is a Greek word, אלון meaning 'another': while he was keeping mourning for Deborah, the news of his mother's death came.

sources.quote: לא נכתב אלא מפני שכל המקומות שהלך יעקב בחזרתו הולך ומפרש
sources.says: Rashbam says it is written only because Scripture goes on listing every place Jacob stopped on his return.

35:10.headline: ישראל replaces 'ambusher', or is added to it
35:10.body: Rashi says יעקב hints at someone who lies in ambush, while ישראל means a prince and leader. Ibn Ezra, Chizkuni and Ramban say 'no longer Jacob' means not Jacob alone: he keeps both names.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן אָדָם הַבָּא בְּמַאֲרָב וְעָקְבָּה, אֶלָּא לְשׁוֹן שַׂר וְנָגִיד
sources.says: Rashi says Jacob is a word for a man who comes in ambush and trickery, but Israel is a word for a prince and leader.

sources.quote: לא יקרא שמך עוד יעקב. לבדו כי גם ישראל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says 'no longer Jacob' means Jacob alone, because it is also Israel.

sources.quote: לא יקרא שמך עוד יעקב לבד כי שני שמות יהיו לך יעקב וישראל
sources.says: Chizkuni says 'not called Jacob alone', because you will have two names, Jacob and Israel.

sources.quote: לֹא שֶׁיֵּאָסֵר לְהִקָּרֵא יַעֲקֹב
sources.says: Ramban says it does not mean he is forbidden to be called Jacob.

35:11.headline: אל שדי: 'God who is enough', and 'strong'
35:11.body: Rashi again hears שדי as 'enough': God says He is enough to bless, for the blessings are His. Radak reads it as 'strong, the one who overcomes nature', since the three mothers were barren and still had children.

sources.quote: שֶׁאֲנִי כְדַי לְבָרֵךְ, שֶׁהַבְּרָכוֹת שֶׁלִּי
sources.says: Rashi says it means that I am enough to bless, for the blessings are mine.

sources.quote: חָזָק, מְנַצֵּחַ הַתּוֹלָדוֹת
sources.says: Radak says it means strong, the One who overcomes the natural course of births.

35:13.headline: Rashi cannot say why 'where He spoke with him' is repeated
35:13.body: This phrase comes up again and again in the passage, and Rashi says he does not know what it teaches. Radak says it tells us this was a place where the divine presence was received and prophecy came.

sources.quote: במקום אשר דבר אתו. אֵינִי יוֹדֵעַ מַה מְּלַמְּדֵנוּ
sources.says: Rashi says, on 'in the place where He spoke with him', that he does not know what it teaches us.

sources.quote: לְהוֹדִיעַ כִּי אוֹתוֹ הַמָּקוֹם הָיָה מְקוֹם קִבּוּל הַשְּׁכִינָה וּמְקוֹם הַנְּבוּאָה
sources.says: Radak says it is to let us know that this place was a place for receiving the divine presence and a place of prophecy.

35:13.headline: 'God went up from him' means the revelation ended
35:13.body: God does not move through space. Maimonides says that when the Bible says God 'goes down' it means a revelation or His presence settles, and 'goes up' means the revelation ends, and he lists this verse as an example.

sources.quote: כינה את ירידת ההתגלות על הנביא או שריית השכינה במקום מסוים "ירידה", ואת הסתלקותו של מצב הנבואה מן האדם או סילוק השכינה "עליה
sources.says: Maimonides says that the revelation coming down on the prophet or the presence resting in a place is called 'going down', and the end of the prophetic state or the removal of the presence is called 'going up'.

sources.quote: וַיַּעַל מֵעָלָיו אֱלֹהִים" (בראשית לה,יג
sources.says: Maimonides lists 'and God went up from him' among his examples.

35:16.headline: כברת הארץ is a distance no one can pin down
35:16.body: The word is rare. Menahem links it to 'much', a long way, Rashi says it is a measure of ground of about a parsa or more, Ibn Ezra says the כ means 'about' and ברת is a king's measure with no other example, and Radak says it means a mile.

sources.quote: מְנַחֵם פֵּרֵשׁ לְשׁוֹן כַּבִּיר, רִבּוּי, מַהֲלָךְ רַב
sources.says: Rashi says Menahem explained it as from 'mighty', meaning many, a long walk.

sources.quote: וְאוֹמֵר אֲנִי שֶׁהוּא שֵׁם מִדַּת קַרְקַע, כְּמוֹ מַהֲלַךְ פַּרְסָה אוֹ יוֹתֵר
sources.says: Rashi says his own view is that it is the name of a measure of ground, like a walk of a parsa or more.

sources.quote: יתכן להיות הכ"ף לדמות ויהיה ברת מדת המלך ואין ריע לו במקרא
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the כ may mean 'like', and ברת is the king's measure, and it has no equal in Scripture.

sources.quote: פֵּרְשׁוּ בּוֹ מִיל
sources.says: Radak says they explained it as a mile.

35:17.headline: 'This one too is a son': Rachel's prayer is answered
35:17.body: The midwife tells Rachel 'this too is a son'. Rashi says 'too' means this one is added to Joseph, and Radak and Rashbam say it echoes Rachel's own prayer at Joseph's birth: 'may the LORD add another son'.

sources.quote: נוֹסַף לְךָ עַל יוֹסֵף
sources.says: Rashi says this one is added to you on top of Joseph.

sources.quote: כִּי גַם זֶה לָךְ בֵּן. כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַרְתְּ ״יֹסֵף ה׳ לִי בֵּן אַחֵר
sources.says: Radak says it is as you said, 'may the LORD add another son for me', and so it was.

sources.quote: כאשר התפללת יוסף ה' לי בן אחר ולא חפץ להמיתך אלא קבל תפילתך
sources.says: Rashbam says as you prayed, 'may the LORD add another son for me', He did not wish to kill you but accepted your prayer.

35:18.headline: בן אוני means 'son of my sorrow'
35:18.body: Rachel names him as she is dying. Rashi says אוני means 'my pain', and Ibn Ezra says 'my mourning', with other verses where the same word is used for mourning.

sources.quote: בן אוני. בֶּן צַעֲרִי
sources.says: Rashi says 'son of my oni' means son of my pain.

sources.quote: בן אוני. בן אבלי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says 'son of my oni' means son of my mourning.

35:22.headline: 'He lay with her': Scripture counts it so for moving the bed
35:22.body: Rashi, from the sages, says that after Rachel died Jacob's bed was moved into Bilhah's tent, and Reuben stood up for his mother Leah and moved it, so Scripture counts it as if he had lain with her. Bahya adds that the sages said anyone who says Reuben sinned is mistaken.

sources.quote: מִתּוֹךְ שֶׁבִּלְבֵּל מִשְׁכָּבוֹ, מַעֲלֶה עָלָיו הַכָּתוּב כְּאִלּוּ שְׁכָבָהּ
sources.says: Rashi says that because he disturbed his bed, Scripture counts it against him as if he had lain with her.

sources.quote: כָּל הָאוֹמֵר רְאוּבֵן חָטָא אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא טוֹעֶה
sources.says: Bahya quotes the sages: anyone who says Reuben sinned is simply wrong.

35:22.headline: פילגש: Reuben may have thought Bilhah was not a full wife
35:22.body: Radak says Reuben may have reasoned that since Bilhah had been a maid, and was then taken as a פילגש, she was not forbidden to him. But the Torah says she was Jacob's wife, so she was forbidden.

sources.quote: אֵשֶׁת אָבִיו הָיְתָה נִקְרֵאת פִּילֶגֶשׁ; שֶׁרְאוּבֵן חָשַׁב כִּי לֹא הָיְתָה אֲסוּרָה עָלָיו לְפִי שֶׁהָיְתָה תְּחִלָּה שִׁפְחָה וְאַחַר כֵּן לְקָחָהּ אָבִיו לְפִילֶגֶשׁ
sources.says: Radak says his father's wife was called a פילגש, because Reuben thought she was not forbidden to him, since she had been a maid first and then his father took her as a פילגש.

35:23.headline: Reuben is still called 'firstborn', even after his sin
35:23.body: Rashi says Scripture calls him firstborn even at the time of his failing, firstborn for inheritance, for service, and for counting, with the extra share going to Joseph only for the tribes. Radak quotes the midrash that he lost the money, not the standing.

sources.quote: אֲפִלּוּ בִּשְׁעַת הַקַּלְקָלָה קְרָאוֹ בְּכוֹר
sources.says: Rashi says even at the time of the wrongdoing, Scripture called him firstborn.

sources.quote: בְּכוֹר לַנַּחֲלָה, בְּכוֹר לָעֲבוֹדָה, בְּכוֹר לְמִנְיָן, וְלֹא נִתְּנָה בְכוֹרָה לְיוֹסֵף אֶלָּא לְעִנְיַן הַשְּׁבָטִים
sources.says: Rashi says firstborn for inheritance, firstborn for service, firstborn for the count, and the birthright was given to Joseph only for the tribes.

sources.quote: בְּכוֹרַת מָמוֹן נִטְּלָה מִמֶּנּוּ וְלֹא נִטְּלָה מִמֶּנּוּ בְּכוֹרַת יוּחֲסִין
sources.says: Radak quotes the midrash: the firstborn's money share was taken from him, but not the firstborn's line of descent.

35:26.headline: 'Born to him in Paddan Aram', though Benjamin was not
35:26.body: The list includes Benjamin, born in Canaan, and Ibn Ezra and Radak say Scripture follows the majority. Chizkuni adds that Benjamin was born in answer to the prayer Rachel prayed in Paddan Aram.

sources.quote: עשתי עשר נולדו לו שם, כי בנימין נולד בארץ כנען, והכתוב כתב על הרוב
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says eleven were born to him there, since Benjamin was born in Canaan, and Scripture writes by the majority.

sources.quote: וְאָמַר בְּפַדַּן אֲרָם אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁבִּנְיָמִין לֹא נוֹלַד בְּפַדַּן אֲרָם, הָלַךְ אַחַר הָרֹב
sources.says: Radak says it says Paddan Aram although Benjamin was not born there, going after the majority.

sources.quote: אשר ילד לו על פי התפלה שנתפללה רחל בפדן ארם שאמרה יוסף ה׳‎ לי בן אחר
sources.says: Chizkuni says it means born to him through the prayer Rachel prayed in Paddan Aram, when she said 'may the LORD add another son'.

35:29.headline: Esau is named first at Isaac's burial
35:29.body: Radak and Rashbam say Esau comes first because he was the firstborn, even though he sold the birthright, and Jacob kept giving him honor. At Abraham's burial Isaac is named before Ishmael, because he was the son of the free woman.

sources.quote: הִקְדִּים עֵשָׂו לְפִי שֶׁהָיָה בְּכוֹר, וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁמָּכַר בְּכֹרָתוֹ, יַעֲקֹב הָיָה נוֹהֵג בּוֹ כָּבוֹד וּמַקְדִּימוֹ לְפָנָיו
sources.says: Radak says he put Esau first because he was the firstborn, and although he sold his birthright, Jacob treated him with honor and put him first.

sources.quote: לפי שהיה בכור ויעקב היה חולק לו כבוד הקדימו הכתוב
sources.says: Rashbam says Scripture put him first because he was the firstborn and Jacob gave him honor.

36:2.headline: עדה was also called בשמת, 'spice'
36:2.body: Esau's wife has two names, and Rashi says she was also called Basemath because she burned spices to idols. Radak says each of Esau's wives had two names, which Scripture often does.

sources.quote: הִיא בָּשְׂמַת בַּת אֵילוֹן, וְנִקְרֵאת בָּשְׂמַת עַל שֵׁם שֶׁהָיְתָה מְקַטֶּרֶת בְּשָׂמִים לַעֲ"זָ
sources.says: Rashi says she is Basemath daughter of Elon, called Basemath because she burned spices to idols.

sources.quote: כִּי שְׁנֵי שֵׁמוֹת הָיוּ לְכָל אַחַת מֵהֶן, וְהַרְבֵּה נִמְצָאִים בַּמִּקְרָא כָּזֶה
sources.says: Radak says each of them had two names, and there are many such cases in Scripture.

36:2.headline: אהליבמה is the same woman as 'Judith'
36:2.body: Rashi says Esau's wife Oholibamah is the Judith named earlier. He says Esau gave her the name יהודית to suggest she rejected idolatry, so as to fool his father.

sources.quote: הִיא יְהוּדִית, וְהוּא כִנָּה שְׁמָהּ יְהוּדִית לוֹמַר שֶׁהִיא כּוֹפֶרֶת בַּעֲ"זָ כְּדֵי לְהַטְעוֹת אֶת אָבִיו
sources.says: Rashi says she is Judith, and he gave her the name Judith to say that she rejects idolatry, in order to mislead his father.

36:2.headline: 'Daughter of Anah, daughter of Zibeon': whose daughter is she?
36:2.body: Anah was Zibeon's son. Rashi says the verse means Zibeon had a child with his son's wife, and the child was Oholibamah, while Ibn Ezra says the verse names both father and grandfather to tell this Anah apart from another Anah.

sources.quote: מְלַמֵּד שֶׁבָּא צִבְעוֹן עַל כַּלָּתוֹ אֵשֶׁת עֲנָה, וְיָצְאָה אָהֳלִיבָמָה מִבֵּין שְׁנֵיהֶם
sources.says: Rashi says it teaches that Zibeon lay with his daughter-in-law, Anah's wife, and Oholibamah came from the two of them.

sources.quote: ויתכן להיות זאת אהליבמה בת ענה שהוא בן צבעון ויחסה הכתוב לשם אביה ואבי אביה להפריש בין ענה ובין ענה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it may be that this Oholibamah is daughter of Anah son of Zibeon, and Scripture traced her to her father and grandfather to tell apart the two Anahs.

36:3.headline: בשמת is called מחלת in chapter 28: 'forgiven'
36:3.body: Ishmael's daughter has two names. Rashi says she was called מחלת, 'forgiven', because the sages teach that three are forgiven their sins: a convert, one who rises to greatness, and one who marries, and Bereshit Rabbah, quoted by Ramban, says בשמת means Esau's mind became fragrant.

sources.quote: לְכָךְ נִקְרֵאת מָחֲלַת, שֶׁנִּמְחֲלוּ עֲוֹנוֹתָיו
sources.says: Rashi says she was called Mahalath because his sins were forgiven.

sources.quote: נָתַן עֵשָׂו דַּעְתּוֹ לְהִתְגַּיֵּר, מָחֲלַת שֶׁמָּחַל לוֹ הקב"ה עַל עֲוֹנֹתָיו, בָּשְׂמַת שֶׁנִּתְבַּשְּׂמָה דַּעְתּוֹ עָלָיו
sources.says: Ramban quotes Bereshit Rabbah: Esau set his mind on converting; Mahalath because the Holy One forgave his sins, Basemath because his mind was perfumed over it.

36:6.headline: Esau 'went to a land': which land?
36:6.body: The verse does not name where Esau went. Rashi says he went to live wherever he would find a place, while Ramban and Bahya say it means the land of Seir, with the name left out because it is understood.

sources.quote: וילך אל ארץ. לָגוּר בַּאֲשֶׁר יִמְצָא
sources.says: Rashi says 'he went to a land' means to live wherever he would find.

sources.quote: וְהַנָּכוֹן בְּעֵינַי שֶׁיֹּאמַר וַיֵּלֶךְ אֶל אֶרֶץ שֵׂעִיר, וְחִסְּרוֹ הַכִּנּוּי בַּעֲבוּר הֱיוֹתוֹ מוּבָן
sources.says: Ramban says the right reading is 'he went to the land of Seir', and the name is left out because it is understood.

sources.quote: וַיֵּלֶךְ אֶל אֶרֶץ שֵׂעִיר כִּי שָׁם הָיָה מְקוֹמוֹ
sources.says: Bahya says it means he went to the land of Seir, because that was his place.

36:12.headline: Why the verse says Timna was only a concubine
36:12.body: Rashi, from the sages, says it shows Abraham's greatness: Timna was a daughter of chiefs, yet she said she was not worthy to marry into the family and asked only to be a concubine. Sforno gives a different picture, that Eliphaz was a conqueror and took her by force.

sources.quote: לְהוֹדִיעַ גְּדֻלָּתוֹ שֶׁל אַבְרָהָם, כַּמָּה הָיוּ תְאֵבִים לִדַּבֵּק בְּזַרְעוֹ. תִּמְנַע זוֹ בַּת אַלּוּפִים הָיְתָה
sources.says: Rashi says it is to make known Abraham's greatness, how eager they were to attach themselves to his seed: this Timna was a daughter of chiefs.

sources.quote: אָמְרָה אֵינִי זוֹכָה לְהִנָּשֵׂא לְךָ, הַלְוַאי וְאֶהְיֶה פִּילֶגֶשׁ
sources.says: Rashi says she said: I do not deserve to marry you, if only I could be a concubine.

sources.quote: שֶׁהָיָה אֱלִיפַז מֵהַכּוֹבְשִׁים אֶת הָאָרֶץ, וְלָקַח אֶת תִּמְנַע אֲחוֹת הָאַלּוּפִים, וְכָבַשׁ אוֹתָהּ לְפִילֶגֶשׁ
sources.says: Sforno says Eliphaz was one of the conquerors of the land, and took Timna, the chiefs' sister, and subdued her as a concubine.

36:15.headline: אלוף means 'chief', and is not 'tame lamb'
36:15.body: Rashi says it means heads of families, and Rashbam adds that all the chiefs in this chapter are rulers of towns and clans. Ibn Ezra says it means a prince or great man, and denies the link to another verse where it means a tame lamb.

sources.quote: אלה אלופי בני עשו. רָאשֵׁי מִשְׁפָּחוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says 'these are the chiefs of the sons of Esau' means heads of families.

sources.quote: כל אלופים שבפרשה משרי עיירות ומשפחות
sources.says: Rashbam says all the chiefs in the passage are rulers of towns and families.

sources.quote: ופי' אלוף נשיא וגדול ואינו כן "ככבש אלוף
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says אלוף means a prince and a great one, and is not like 'like a tame lamb'.

36:20.headline: Why list the sons of Seir at all?
36:20.body: To a reader the list looks pointless, but Maimonides says it matters for one commandment: only Amalek was to be wiped out, and the list shows that the people living in Seir are not all Amalek's descendants. Ibn Ezra, quoted by Ramban, also says it separates Seir's family from Esau's.

sources.quote: תיאור שבטי בני שעיר וייחוסם האישי הוא בשל מצוה אחת: שהוא יתעלה ציווה למחות את זרע עמלק דווקא
sources.says: Maimonides says the description of Seir's tribes and their descent is for one commandment: that God commanded to wipe out the seed of Amalek in particular.

sources.quote: הִזְכִּיר הַכָּתוּב זֶה לְהַפְרִישׁ יִחוּסֵי שֵׂעִיר וְעֵשָׂו, כִּי יִשְׂרָאֵל יְצֻוּוּ עַל בְּנֵי עֵשָׂו
sources.says: Ramban quotes Ibn Ezra: Scripture mentioned this to set apart the lines of Seir and Esau, since Israel will be commanded about the sons of Esau.

36:20.headline: החרי: a nobleman, a man's name, or a people?
36:20.body: Ibn Ezra reads החורי as 'noble', like the nobles of Judah in Jeremiah. Ramban says it is the name of a man, an ancestor, like Amorite and Perizzite.

sources.quote: החורי, כמו חורי יהודה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says החורי is like 'the nobles of Judah'.

sources.quote: וטעמו גדולה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says its meaning is greatness.

sources.quote: הַחֹרִי שֵׁם אִישׁ הָיָה אֲבִי אֻמָּה קַדְמוֹנִית תִּקָּרֵא עַל שְׁמוֹ כְּמוֹ הָאֱמוֹרִי וְהַפְּרִזִּי
sources.says: Ramban says החרי was the name of a man, the father of an ancient nation, named for him like the Amorite and Perizzite.

36:20.headline: 'Inhabitants of the land' also means 'experts at settling it'
36:20.body: The plain meaning is that they lived there before Esau came. The sages hear a second meaning, that they were skilled at settling the land and could taste the soil to tell which plant would grow in it.

sources.quote: שֶׁהָיוּ יוֹשְׁבֶיהָ קֹדֶם שֶׁבָּא עֵשָׂו לְשָׁם
sources.says: Rashi says they were its inhabitants before Esau came there.

sources.quote: שֶׁהָיוּ בְּקִיאִין בְּיִשּׁוּבָהּ שֶׁל אֶרֶץ; מְלֹא קָנֶה זֶה לְזֵיתִים, מְלֹא קָנֶה זֶה לִגְפָנִים
sources.says: Rashi says the sages taught that they were expert at settling the land: this reedful of soil is for olives, this one for vines.

36:22.headline: 'Lotan's sister was Timna': a verse that looked pointless
36:22.body: Rashbam says Timna is called Lotan's sister because he was the oldest of the brothers. The Talmud, quoted by Maimonides, tells of the wicked King Manasseh, who mocked this verse and said Moses should have written only this one, but Maimonides answers that every story in the Torah has a purpose.

sources.quote: לפי שהיה גדול שבאחיו קורא לה אחות לוטן
sources.says: Rashbam says that since he was the eldest of his brothers, she is called Lotan's sister.

sources.quote: לא היה לו למשה לכתוב אלא 'וַאֲחוֹת לוֹטָן תִּמְנָע
