sources.quote: דָּבָר שָׂנְאוּי הוּא לַמִּצְרִים לֶאֱכֹל אֶת הָעִבְרִים, וְאֻנְקְלוֹס נָתַן טַעַם לַדָּבָר
sources.says: Rashi says it is something hateful to the Egyptians, to eat with the Hebrews, and that Onkelos gave a reason for it.

sources.quote: אֲרֵי בְעִירָא דְּמִצְרָאֵי דָחֲלִין לֵיהּ עִבְרָאֵי אָכְלִין
sources.says: Onkelos says the Hebrews eat the animal the Egyptians fear.

sources.quote: בזוי היא למצרים לאכול עם אנשי עבר הנהר
sources.says: Rashbam says it is despised by the Egyptians to eat with people from across the river.

43:34.headline: 'Five hands' means five portions: whose?
43:34.body: Rashi says ידות means portions, and counts five for Benjamin: his own with the brothers, and Joseph's, Asenath's, Manasseh's and Ephraim's. Ibn Ezra says it only means portions.

sources.quote: חֶלְקוֹ עִם אֶחָיו, וּמַשְׂאַת יוֹסֵף וְאָסְנַת וּמְנַשֶּׁה וְאֶפְרַיִם
sources.says: Rashi says his share with his brothers, plus the portions of Joseph, Asenath, Manasseh and Ephraim.

sources.quote: ידות. חלקים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says ידות means portions.

43:34.headline: 'They were merry' hints they had not drunk since the sale
43:34.body: Rashi says from the day they sold Joseph, neither they nor he drank wine. On that day they drank.

sources.quote: וּמִיּוֹם שֶׁמְּכָרוּהוּ לֹא שָׁתוּ יַיִן וְלֹא הוּא שָׁתָה יַיִן, וְאוֹתוֹ הַיּוֹם שָׁתוּ
sources.says: Rashi says from the day they sold him they did not drink wine, and neither did he, and on that day they drank.

44:3.headline: In 'the morning אור', אור is a verb: it grew light
44:3.body: The word looks like the noun 'light', but here it is a verb meaning 'it was light'. Radak and Rashbam both stop to say so, and compare 'my eyes אורו', 'lit up'.

sources.quote: הַבֹּקֶר אוֹר. פֹּעַל עָבָר מִגִּזְרַת פָּעוּל
sources.says: Radak says אור here is a past-tense verb, like אֹרוּ in 'my eyes were bright'.

sources.quote: הבקר אור - האיר, כמו: ראו נא כי אורו עיני לשעבר
sources.says: Rashbam says אור means האיר, 'it lit up', like אורו in 'see how my eyes have lit up'.

44:4.headline: את here means 'out of', not its usual object marker
44:4.body: The small word את usually marks the object of a verb. Radak says that here it means 'from': they left the city.

sources.quote: אֶת הָעִיר. מִן הָעִיר, וְכֵן ״כְּצֵאתִי אֶת הָעִיר״
sources.says: Radak says את הָעִיר means 'from the city', and gives 'when I leave the city' as another example.

44:5.headline: Joseph says he 'divines' with the cup, but it may mean 'tested'
44:5.body: The verb נחש usually means reading signs, as in magic, but Ibn Ezra says here it means to test: Joseph set out the cup to see if they would steal. Radak reports another view, that Joseph would ask diviners who took it.

sources.quote: הוא נסה אתכם בו לדעת אם אתם גנבים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says Joseph tested them with the cup to learn whether they were thieves.

sources.quote: יֵשׁ מְפָרְשִׁים: יִשְׁאַל לַמְנַחֲשִׁים בַּעֲבוּרוֹ מִי לְקָחוֹ
sources.says: Radak says some explain that Joseph would ask diviners who took the cup.

44:7.headline: 'Far be it' may come from חולין, the word for 'profane'
44:7.body: Rashi stops on חלילה to give its root: it comes from חולין, 'profane', and is a word of disgust. He adds that Onkelos translates it חס, 'God forbid'.

sources.quote: חֻלִּין הוּא לָנוּ, לְשׁוֹן גְּנַאי, וְתַרְגוּם חַס לְעַבְדָּיךְ
sources.says: Rashi says חלילה means 'this is profane to us', a word of disgrace, and that Onkelos renders it חס.

44:15.headline: Rashi reads Joseph's 'divining' as clever reasoning, not magic
44:15.body: Joseph says a man like him can נחש the thief. Rashi says this means working it out by knowledge and reasoning, while Rashbam says it was the way of rulers to practise divination.

sources.quote: יוֹדֵעַ לְנַחֵשׁ וְלָדַעַת מִדַּעַת וּמִסְּבָרָא וּבִינָה
sources.says: Rashi says an important man like Joseph knows how to work things out from knowledge, reason and understanding.

sources.quote: כי דרך השרים לקסום קסם
sources.says: Rashbam says it was the way of nobles to use divination.

44:16.headline: Why נצטדק has an odd ט: it comes from צדק, 'right'
44:16.body: The word is a reflexive form of צדק, 'right', and the ט stands in for a ת because of the צ. Judah is asking how they could prove themselves in the right.

sources.quote: נִצְטַדָּק מִגִּזְרַת צדק
sources.says: Rashi says נצטדק comes from the root צדק and explains the ט in it.

sources.quote: תחת תי"ו התפעל בעבור הצדי"ק
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the ט stands in the place of the ת of the reflexive form because of the צ.

sources.quote: לֹא נוּכַל לוֹמַר שֶׁאֲנַחְנוּ צַדִּיקִים בָּזֶה
sources.says: Radak says the brothers cannot claim to be in the right over the cup.

44:16.headline: How can God 'find' a sin the brothers did not commit?
44:16.body: Judah says God 'found' their guilt, though they know they did not steal. Rashi says a creditor found his chance to collect an old debt, and Ibn Ezra says it is a figure of speech for a forgotten sin now found.

sources.quote: מָצָא בַּעַל חוֹב מָקוֹם לִגְבּוֹת שְׁטַר חוֹבוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says a creditor has found a place to collect on his note.

sources.quote: על דרך משל, כי עון היה לנו וכאלו נשכח ואיננו והיום נמצא
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is a figure of speech: they had a sin that seemed forgotten, and today it was found.

44:18.headline: ויגש can mean 'came near' for war, peace, or prayer
44:18.body: The sages in Bereshit Rabbah ask why Judah 'drew near': to fight, to make peace, or to pray. Maimonides says the first sense of this verb is simple movement toward a person, and he cites this very verse.

sources.quote: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר הֲגָשָׁה לְמִלְחָמָה, הֵיךְ מָה דְאַתְּ אָמַר (שמואל ב י, יג): וַיִּגַּשׁ יוֹאָב וְהָעָם אֲשֶׁר עִמּוֹ לַמִּלְחָמָה, רַבִּי נְחֶמְיָה אוֹמֵר הֲגָשָׁה לְפִיּוּס
sources.says: The midrash gives three views: Judah drew near for war, for appeasement, or for prayer.

sources.quote: ומשמעותה הראשונה של "נגישה" היא התקדמות אדם אחד אל אחר ותנועתו אליו
sources.says: Maimonides says the first meaning of נגישה is one person moving toward another, and gives this verse as the example.

44:18.headline: 'Like Pharaoh' is respect on the surface and a threat underneath
44:18.body: On the plain reading Judah says Joseph is as great as the king. Rashi adds a midrash that hears a warning: Joseph will be struck as Pharaoh was for holding Sarah one night.

sources.quote: וּמִדְרָשׁוֹ סוֹפְךָ לִלְקוֹת עָלָיו בְּצָרַעַת כְּמוֹ שֶׁלָּקָה פַרְעֹה עַל יְדֵי זְקֵנָתִי שָׂרָה עַל לַיְלָה אַחַת שֶׁעִכְּבָהּ
sources.says: Rashi gives a midrash that Joseph will be struck with leprosy, as Pharaoh was for holding Sarah one night.

sources.quote: אתה כמלך והמלך כמוך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the plain sense is that Joseph is like the king and the king is like Joseph.

44:21.headline: 'Set my eye on him' may mean to look, or to protect
44:21.body: The phrase can mean just 'see him' (Ibn Ezra), or 'watch over him kindly' (Ramban, who cites Jeremiah). Rashi has Judah throw it back at Joseph: is this your 'setting an eye'?

sources.quote: שאראה אותו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means that I may see him.

sources.quote: וְלֹא מָצָאתִי בַּכָּתוּב שִׂימַת עַיִן עַל הָרְאִיָּה בִּלְבַד
sources.says: Ramban says he finds no verse where 'setting an eye' means only seeing; it means to guard and do good.

sources.quote: וְכִי זוֹ הִיא שִׂימַת עַיִן שֶׁאָמַרְתָּ לָשׂוּם עֵינְךָ עָלָיו
sources.says: Rashi has Judah ask whether this is the 'setting of an eye' Joseph promised.

44:29.headline: אסון is a rare word for a death that comes by chance
44:29.body: Jacob fears אסון will strike Benjamin on the road. Ramban says it means a chance death, such as from wild animals or a change in the air, and Rashi adds that Satan accuses at a time of danger.

sources.quote: פֵּרוּשׁ אָסוֹן – מָוֶת מִקְרִית, כְּמֵתִים בִּידֵי אָדָם וְחַיָּה רָעָה אוֹ בְּשִׁנּוּי הָאֲוִיר בַּדֶּרֶךְ
sources.says: Ramban says אסון means a death by chance, such as at the hands of people, wild animals, or a change of air on the road.

sources.quote: שֶׁהַשָּׂטָן מְקַטְרֵג בִּשְׁעַת הַסַּכָּנָה
sources.says: Rashi says that Satan accuses in a time of danger.

45:2.headline: 'House of Pharaoh' is his servants here, but a real house later
45:2.body: Rashi says בית in verse 2 means Pharaoh's people, as in 'house of Israel', not a building. In verse 16 the same words do mean the house itself.

sources.quote: וְאֵין זֶה לְשׁוֹן בַּיִת מַמָּשׁ, אֶלָּא כְמוֹ בֵּית יִשְׂרָאֵל, בֵּית יְהוּדָה
sources.says: Rashi says בית here is not a literal house but means the household, like 'house of Israel' or 'house of Judah'.

sources.quote: כְּמוֹ בְּבֵית פַּרְעֹה, וְזֶהוּ לְשׁוֹן בַּיִת מַמָּשׁ
sources.says: Rashi says that in verse 16 the word means the actual house.

45:3.headline: The brothers' terror is a warning about facing God's judgment
45:3.body: The brothers could not answer Joseph because they were terrified. Rashi says it was from shame, and Bereshit Rabbah says that if they could not stand Joseph's rebuke, no one can stand God's.

sources.quote: נבהלו מפניו. מִפְּנֵי הַבּוּשָׁה
sources.says: Rashi says they were terrified because of shame.

sources.quote: אוֹי לָנוּ מִיּוֹם הַדִּין אוֹי לָנוּ מִיּוֹם הַתּוֹכֵחָה
sources.says: The midrash says: woe to us on the day of judgment, for the brothers could not stand Joseph's rebuke, and God's will be far greater.

45:4.headline: 'Come near' was said gently, and he showed he was circumcised
45:4.body: Rashi says Joseph saw his brothers shrinking back and called them close in a soft voice. He adds, from Bereshit Rabbah, that Joseph showed them he was circumcised, as proof of who he was.

sources.quote: רָאָה אוֹתָם נְסוֹגִים לְאָחוֹר, אָמַר עַכְשָׁו אַחַי נִכְלָמִים, קָרָא לָהֶם בְּלָשׁוֹן רַכָּה וְתַחֲנוּנִים, וְהֶרְאָה לָהֶם שֶׁהוּא מָהוּל
sources.says: Rashi says Joseph saw them pulling back, called them in a gentle, pleading voice, and showed them he was circumcised.

sources.quote: גְּשׁוּ נָא אֵלַי וַיִּגָּשׁוּ, הֶרְאָה לָהֶם אֶת הַמִּילָה
sources.says: The midrash says that at 'come near to me' Joseph showed them the covenant of circumcision.

45:7.headline: Joseph says God 'sent' him, though his brothers sold him
45:7.body: Maimonides says Scripture often says God 'sent' or 'commanded' something when the nearest cause was human choice or chance. He names Joseph's words in verses 7 and 8 as examples.

sources.quote: ובמעשה יוסף: "וַיִּשְׁלָחֵנִי אֱלֹהִים לִפְנֵיכֶם
sources.says: Maimonides lists Joseph's 'God sent me before you' among events that happen by chance but are described as God's doing.

sources.quote: ויוסף הצדיק אמר: "לֹא אַתֶּם שְׁלַחְתֶּם אֹתִי הֵנָּה כִּי הָאֱלֹהִים"
sources.says: Maimonides gives Joseph's 'it was not you who sent me here but God' as an example of a human choice described as God's act.

45:8.headline: Joseph is 'a father to Pharaoh': a patron or a teacher
45:8.body: Joseph is not Pharaoh's real father. Rashi says לאב means a friend and patron, and Ibn Ezra says it means a teacher, as in 'father of all who' in Genesis 4:21.

sources.quote: לאב. לְחָבֵר וּלְפַטְרוֹן
sources.says: Rashi says לאב means a companion and a patron.

sources.quote: לאב. טעמו למורה וכן "אבי כל תופש"
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says לאב means a teacher, like 'father of all who handle the harp' in Genesis 4:21.

45:11.headline: תורש looks like 'inherit' but here means 'be left poor'
45:11.body: The root ירש usually means to inherit or take over. Here Rashi and Rashbam read it the other way round: to be stripped of what you have, or driven out.

sources.quote: דִּלְמָא תִּתְמַסְכַּן, לְשׁוֹן מוֹרִישׁ וּמַעֲשִׁיר
sources.says: Rashi says it means 'lest you become poor', as in the phrase that God makes poor and makes rich.

sources.quote: תתגרש מן הארץ ע"י רעבון
sources.says: Rashbam says it means you would be driven out of the land by the famine.

45:12.headline: 'My mouth speaks to you' means in their own language
45:12.body: Joseph says it is his own mouth speaking to them. Rashi says he spoke in Hebrew, and Radak says he spoke in their own language with no interpreter, as there had been until now.

sources.quote: וְעוֹד, כי פי המדבר אליכם בִּלְשׁוֹן הַקֹּדֶשׁ
sources.says: Rashi says 'my mouth speaks to you' means in the holy tongue, Hebrew.

sources.quote: וְעַד עַתָּה הָיָה הַמֵּלִיץ בֵּינוֹתֵינוּ, שֶׁהָיִיתִי מְכַסֶּה עַצְמִי מִכֶּם
sources.says: Radak says that until now an interpreter stood between them, while Joseph hid who he was.

45:14.headline: Benjamin has one neck, but the verse says 'necks'
45:14.body: The sages read the plural 'necks' as the two Temples that would stand in Benjamin's land, and Benjamin's weeping on Joseph's 'necks' as the tent at Shiloh in Joseph's land. Both would later be destroyed.

sources.quote: וְכִי שְׁנֵי צַוָּארִים הָיוּ לוֹ לְבִנְיָמִין
sources.says: The midrash asks whether Benjamin had two necks.

sources.quote: עַל שְׁנֵי מִקְדָּשׁוֹת שֶׁעֲתִידִין לִהְיוֹת בְּחֶלְקוֹ שֶׁל בִּנְיָמִין וְסוֹפָן לֵחָרֵב
sources.says: Rashi says Joseph wept for the two Temples that would be in Benjamin's portion and would be destroyed.

sources.quote: עַל מִשְׁכַּן שִׁילֹה שֶׁעָתִיד לִהְיוֹת בְּחֶלְקוֹ שֶׁל יוֹסֵף וְסוֹפוֹ לֵחָרֵב
sources.says: Rashi says Benjamin wept for the Tent at Shiloh that would be in Joseph's portion and would be destroyed.

45:17.headline: Does טענו mean 'load up' or 'prod your donkeys'?
45:17.body: This form of טען appears only here. Radak says it means to load, as the rabbis use it, and reports that his father read it as 'prod', to goad the donkeys on.

sources.quote: עִנְיַן מַשָּׂא, וְכֵן בִּדְבָרֵי רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סנהדרין לב) ״אַחַת טְעוּנָה וְאַחַת שֶׁאֵינָהּ טְעוּנָה״. וַאֲדֹנִי אָבִי זְקֵנִי זִכְרוֹנוֹ לִבְרָכָה פֵּרֵשׁ עִנְיַן דְּקִירָה, דִּקְרוּ חֲמוֹרֵיכֶם בְּדָרְבָּן שֶׁלָּהֶם לְמַהֲרָם לָלֶכֶת
sources.says: Radak says it means a load, and reports that his father explained it as prodding the donkeys with a goad to hurry them.

sources.quote: שימו משא ומטעני חרב
sources.says: Ibn Ezra explains it as 'put a load', and says the phrase 'loaded with the sword' in Isaiah is close to it.

45:20.headline: 'Let your eye not pity': pity put in the eye
45:20.body: Pity belongs to the heart, yet the verse puts it in the eye. Radak says this is how the holy language speaks, because the heart feels pity when the eye sees.

sources.quote: מִנְהַג לְשׁוֹן הַקֹּדֶשׁ לִסְמֹךְ הַחֶמְלָה בָּרֹב אֶל הָעַיִן, וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין הַחֶמְלָה אֶלָּא בַּלֵּב
sources.says: Radak says it is Hebrew's habit to link pity to the eye, though pity is really in the heart.

45:23.headline: מזון is a rare word: a relish, or any food at all
45:23.body: Rashi says מזון is a relish to eat with bread, and Ibn Ezra lists beans, lentils, figs, raisins and dates. Bereshit Rabbah says all foods are called מזון.

sources.quote: ומזון. לִפְתָּן
sources.says: Rashi says מזון means a relish eaten with bread.

sources.quote: אפונים ופול ועדשים ודחן וכסמין ותאנים וצמוקים ותמרים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra lists peas, beans, lentils, millet, spelt, figs, raisins and dates.

sources.quote: מָזוֹן, אָמַר רַב אַחָא בַּר אִילָא מִכָּאן שֶׁכָּל הַדְּבָרִים קְרוּיִם מָזוֹן
sources.says: The midrash says that from this verse we learn that all foods are called מזון.

45:24.headline: תרגזו can mean fear, quarrelling, or getting stuck in study
45:24.body: Joseph tells his brothers not to be agitated on the road. Rashi reads it as quarrelling over who caused the sale or as getting lost in study, and Rashbam reads it as fear of robbers.

sources.quote: וּלְפִי פְשׁוּטוֹ שֶׁל מִקְרָא יֵשׁ לוֹמַר, לְפִי שֶׁהָיוּ נִכְלָמִים, הָיָה דוֹאֵג, שֶׁמָּא יָרִיבוּ בַדֶּרֶךְ עַל דְּבַר מְכִירָתוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says that on the plain reading Joseph feared they would quarrel on the road over who was to blame for the sale.

sources.quote: אל תיראו כלום בדרך מפני ליסטים
sources.says: Rashbam says it means do not be afraid of anything on the road, such as robbers.

sources.quote: אַל תִּתְעַסְּקוּ בִּדְבַר הֲלָכָה שֶׁלֹּא תִרְגַּז עֲלֵיכֶם הַדֶּרֶךְ
sources.says: Rashi says one reading is: do not get absorbed in a point of law, so that the road does not become angry with you.

45:26.headline: ויפג: Jacob's heart went numb, or turned away from belief
45:26.body: The verb is rare. Ibn Ezra says Jacob's heart stood still, as if dead, and Rashi says it turned away and would not believe, comparing the Aramaic word פג for a scent that did not change.

sources.quote: והטעם שעמד לבו ודמם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means his heart stood still and went silent.

sources.quote: נֶחֱלַף לִבּוֹ וְהָלַךְ מִלְּהַאֲמִין, לֹא הָיָה לִבּוֹ פוֹנֶה אֶל הַדְּבָרִים
sources.says: Rashi says his heart turned away from believing and did not turn toward what they said.

sources.quote: חָלַשׁ לִבּוֹ וְנִרְפָּה עַל שֶׁזְּכָרוּהוּ
sources.says: Radak says his heart grew weak and limp when they spoke of Joseph.

sources.quote: מְתַּרְגְּמִינַן וְרֵיחֵיהּ לָא פָג
sources.says: Rashi compares the Aramaic translation of 'his scent did not change', which uses the word פג.

45:27.headline: The wagons (עגלות) were a secret sign pointing to the עגלה ערופה
45:27.body: Joseph sent wagons because the word עגלות recalled the last lesson he studied with his father, the עגלה ערופה, the heifer whose neck is broken. Rashi notes the verse says wagons that Joseph sent, not Pharaoh.

sources.quote: סִימָן מָסַר לָהֶם בַּמֶּה הָיָה עוֹסֵק כְּשֶׁפֵּרֵשׁ מִמֶּנּוּ – בְּפָרָשַׁת עֶגְלָה עֲרוּפָה
sources.says: Rashi says Joseph gave a sign: what he was studying when he left his father, the passage of the עגלה ערופה.

sources.quote: לֹא בְּפָרָשַׁת עֶגְלָה עֲרוּפָה הָיִיתִי עוֹסֵק, הֲדָא הוּא דִכְתִיב: וַיַּרְא אֶת הָעֲגָלוֹת
sources.says: The midrash says the brothers were to tell Jacob that Joseph had been studying the עגלה ערופה, as the verse says he saw the wagons.

45:27.headline: 'Jacob's spirit revived' may mean prophecy came back to him
45:27.body: Rashi says the Divine Presence, which had left Jacob, rested on him again. Radak adds the sages' view that prophecy only rests on a person in joy, and Jacob had been in mourning.

sources.quote: שָׁרְתָה עָלָיו שְׁכִינָה, שֶׁפֵּרְשָׁה מִמֶּנּוּ
sources.says: Rashi says the Divine Presence rested on him, having left him.

sources.quote: כִּי אֵין רוּחַ נְבוּאָה שׁוֹרָה אֶלָּא מִתּוֹךְ שִׂמְחָה
sources.says: Radak says the rabbis taught that the spirit of prophecy rests only on a person who is in joy.

45:28.headline: 'Rav' can mean great joy, enough, or Joseph's great strength
45:28.body: Jacob says רב, which can mean 'much' or 'enough'. Rashi reads it as great joy, Rashbam as 'enough, I no longer doubt', and Bereshit Rabbah as the great strength of Joseph.

sources.quote: רַב לִי עוֹד שִׂמְחָה וְחֶדְוָה הוֹאִיל וְעוֹד יוֹסֵף בְּנִי חַי
sources.says: Rashi says it means I have great joy, since my son Joseph is still alive.

sources.quote: די בפוגת לבי שלא האמנתי אלא ודאי עוד יוסף בני חי
sources.says: Rashbam says it means enough of my heart's numbness and disbelief: surely my son Joseph is alive.

sources.quote: רַב כֹּחוֹ שֶׁל יוֹסֵף בְּנִי, שֶׁכַּמָּה צָרוֹת הִגִּיעוּהוּ וַעֲדַיִן הוּא עוֹמֵד בְּצִדְקוֹ
sources.says: The midrash reads it as 'great is the strength of my son Joseph', who kept his righteousness through many troubles.

46:1.headline: Why 'the God of his father Isaac' and not Abraham?
46:1.body: Jacob offers sacrifices to 'the God of his father Isaac'. Rashi says a person owes more honour to a father than to a grandfather, and Radak says Isaac had been told not to go down to Egypt, so Jacob sought God's will first.

sources.quote: חַיָּב אָדָם בִּכְבוֹד אָבִיו יוֹתֵר מִבִּכְבוֹד זְקֵנוֹ, לְפִיכָךְ תָּלָה בְּיִצְחָק וְלֹא בְאַבְרָהָם
sources.says: Rashi says one owes more honour to a father than to a grandfather, so the verse names Isaac, not Abraham.

sources.quote: אָמַר כֵּן לְפִי שֶׁיִּצְחָק אָבִיו הָיָה רְצוֹנוֹ לָרֶדֶת מִצְרַיִם מִפְּנֵי הָרָעָב וְאָמַר לוֹ הָאֵל ״אַל תֵּרֵד מִצְרָיְמָה״
sources.says: Radak says Isaac wanted to go down to Egypt in a famine and God told him not to, which is why Jacob named Isaac's God.

46:2.headline: 'Jacob, Jacob': a loving call, or a call to notice prophecy
46:2.body: God says Jacob's name twice. Rashi says the doubling is a word of affection, and Radak says that after years without prophecy the second call made Jacob realise it was God.

sources.quote: יעקב יעקב. לְשׁוֹן חִבָּה
sources.says: Rashi says the repeated name is an expression of affection.

sources.quote: כָּפַל לוֹ הַקְּרִיאָה, לְפִי שֶׁעָמַד כַּמָּה שָׁנִים שֶׁלֹּא שָׁרְתָה עָלָיו רוּחַ נְבוּאָה
sources.says: Radak says God doubled the call because for many years the spirit of prophecy had not rested on Jacob.

46:2.headline: 'Visions of the night' and 'a dream of the night' differ
46:2.body: Maimonides says God speaking to Jacob 'in the visions of the night' is true prophecy. When God came to Laban or Abimelech 'in a dream of the night', it was not prophecy at all.

sources.quote: והתבונן בהבדל בין דבריו "ויבא אלהים" לבין דבריו "ויאמר אלהים", ובין דבריו "בחלום הלילה" לבין דבריו "במראות הלילה"
sources.says: Maimonides says to notice the difference between 'God came' and 'God said', and between 'in a dream of the night' and 'in the visions of the night'.

46:4.headline: God says 'I will go down with you': Onkelos keeps it literal
46:4.body: Maimonides says Onkelos usually turns any 'God came down' into 'God was revealed', so as not to suggest God moves. Here he leaves 'I will go down' as it stands, because it reports words spoken in a night vision.

sources.quote: כל מונח שהוא מוצא המורה על אחד ממיני התנועה, הוא מפרש את משמעות התנועה כהתגלות וכהופעה של אור נברא
sources.says: Maimonides says Onkelos explains any word of motion said of God as a revelation or an appearance of created light.

sources.quote: מכיוון שבתחילת הדיבור נאמר שהוא היה במראות הלילה, לא חשב אנקלוס לבלתי ראוי לומר כלשונם את הדברים שנאמרו במראות הלילה
sources.says: Maimonides says that because the passage begins with 'visions of the night', Onkelos saw no problem keeping the words as they were spoken.

46:4.headline: 'I will also bring you up': burial, or the whole nation
46:4.body: Rashi and Radak say God promised Jacob he would be brought up for burial in the Land. Radak also reads the second 'up' as his children, and Chizkuni says it takes in the bones of the other tribes.

sources.quote: הִבְטִיחוֹ לִהְיוֹת נִקְבָּר בָּאָרֶץ
sources.says: Rashi says God promised him he would be buried in the Land.

sources.quote: אוֹ פֵּרוּשׁוֹ עַל עַצְמוֹ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה עִמּוֹ כְּשֶׁיַּעֲלוּהוּ לְקִבְרוֹ. וְאָמַר גַּם־עָלֹה, עַל בָּנָיו שֶׁיַּעֲלוּם מִשָּׁם
sources.says: Radak says it may mean God would be with Jacob when he is brought up to his grave, and the 'also' refers to his sons being brought up from Egypt.

sources.quote: גם עלה לרבות עצמות שאר כל השבטים
sources.says: Chizkuni says 'also' adds the bones of all the other tribes.

46:4.headline: 'Joseph will place his hand on your eyes': closing them in death
46:4.body: Ibn Ezra and Chizkuni say this is the custom of closing a dead person's eyes. Chizkuni also offers a second reading: 'eyes' stands for 'affairs', and Joseph will see to what you need.

sources.quote: במותך, כן מנהג החיים עם המתים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means at your death, as the living do for the dead.

sources.quote: ישתדל לעסוק בצרכיך
sources.says: Chizkuni says a second reading is that Joseph will make an effort to take care of Jacob's needs.

46:7.headline: Jacob had one daughter, so who are his 'daughters'?
46:7.body: The verse says 'daughters' though Jacob had only Dinah. Ibn Ezra says it includes girls raised in Dinah's house, Radak says daughters-in-law, and Chizkuni says Scripture simply speaks this way.

sources.quote: היא דינה לבדה ויתכן שהיה לדינה שפחות קטנות גדלו עמה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is Dinah alone, or perhaps also young maidservants who grew up with her.

sources.quote: בְּנֹתָיו. דִּינָה בִּתּוֹ וְכַלּוֹתָיו
sources.says: Radak says 'his daughters' means his daughter Dinah and his daughters-in-law.

sources.quote: אין לו אלא אחת כן דרך הכתוב לדבר
sources.says: Chizkuni says that although he had only one, this is how Scripture speaks.

46:10.headline: Who is 'the Canaanite woman' who was Shaul's mother?
46:10.body: Rashi says it was Dinah, called Canaanite because she had been with a Canaanite. Ibn Ezra says it was a real Canaanite wife, and the verse names her because Simeon should not have married one.

sources.quote: בֶּן דִּינָה שֶׁנִּבְעֲלָה לִכְנַעֲנִי
sources.says: Rashi says Shaul was the son of Dinah, who had been with a Canaanite.

sources.quote: והזכיר זו לבדה בעבור שעשה שמעון שלא כהוגן לקחת כנענית
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the verse names this one wife only because Simeon acted wrongly in taking a Canaanite.

46:15.headline: The verse says thirty-three, but only thirty-two names are listed
46:15.body: Rashi says the missing one is Yocheved, born between the city walls as the family arrived. Ibn Ezra rejects that and says Jacob himself is counted in the total.

sources.quote: וּבִפְרָטָן אִי אַתָּה מוֹצֵא אֶלָּא שְׁלֹשִׁים וּשְׁנַיִם, אֶלָּא זוֹ יוֹכֶבֶד שֶׁנּוֹלְדָה בֵין הַחוֹמוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says the names add up to thirty-two, and the thirty-third is Yocheved, born between the walls.

sources.quote: והנכון בעיני שיעקב בחשבון וממנו יחל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the right reading is that Jacob is in the count and the count starts with him.

46:21.headline: Bela means 'swallowed up': a son named for lost Joseph
46:21.body: Bereshit Rabbah says Benjamin named his ten sons after what happened to his brother Joseph. בלע, Bela, is 'he was swallowed up from me'.

sources.quote: בֶּלַע, שֶׁנִּבְלַע מִמֶּנִּי
sources.says: The midrash says Bela is because Joseph was swallowed up from Benjamin.

46:21.headline: Becher means 'firstborn': a son named for Joseph
46:21.body: Bereshit Rabbah says Benjamin named this son בכר, Becher, because Joseph was a firstborn to him.

sources.quote: בֶּכֶר, שֶׁהָיָה בְּכוֹר לִי
sources.says: The midrash says Becher is because Joseph was a firstborn to Benjamin.

46:21.headline: Ashbel means 'taken captive': a son named for Joseph
46:21.body: Bereshit Rabbah says Benjamin named this son אשבל, Ashbel, because Joseph was taken captive from him.

sources.quote: אַשְׁבֵּל, שֶׁנִּשְׁבָּה מִמֶּנִּי
sources.says: The midrash says Ashbel is because Joseph was taken captive from Benjamin.

46:21.headline: Gera means 'lived as a stranger': a son named for Joseph
46:21.body: Bereshit Rabbah says Benjamin named this son גרא, Gera, because Joseph lived as a stranger in another land.

sources.quote: גֵּרָא, שֶׁגָּר בְּאֶרֶץ אַחֶרֶת
sources.says: The midrash says Gera is because Joseph lived in another land.

46:21.headline: Naaman means 'pleasant': a son named for Joseph's character
46:21.body: Bereshit Rabbah says Benjamin named this son נעמן, Naaman, because Joseph's deeds were pleasant and sweet.

sources.quote: נַעֲמָן, שֶׁהָיוּ מַעֲשָׂיו נָאִים וּנְעִימִים
sources.says: The midrash says Naaman is because Joseph's deeds were fair and pleasant.

46:21.headline: Ehi means 'my brother': a son named for Joseph
46:21.body: Bereshit Rabbah says Benjamin named this son אחי, Ehi, because Joseph was truly his brother.

sources.quote: אֵחִי, שֶׁהָיָה אָחִי וַדַּאי
sources.says: The midrash says Ehi is because Joseph was surely Benjamin's brother.

46:21.headline: Rosh means 'head': a son named for Joseph
46:21.body: Bereshit Rabbah says Benjamin named this son ראש, Rosh, because Joseph was a head to him, and the head of his brothers.

sources.quote: וָרֹאשׁ, שֶׁהָיָה לִי לְרֹאשׁ
sources.says: The midrash says Rosh is because Joseph was a head to Benjamin.

46:21.headline: Muppim: Joseph was handsome and held his fathers' teachings
46:21.body: Bereshit Rabbah says Benjamin named this son מפים, Muppim, because Joseph was very handsome, and because Jacob handed him all the teachings that Shem and Eber had passed down.

sources.quote: מֻפִּים, שֶׁהָיָה יָפֶה מְאֹד בְּכָל דָּבָר, וְשֶׁכָּל הֲלָכוֹת שֶׁמָּסְרוּ שֵׁם וְעֵבֶר לְיַעֲקֹב מְסָרוֹ לוֹ
sources.says: The midrash says Muppim is because Joseph was very handsome, and Jacob passed on to him all that Shem and Eber had passed to Jacob.

46:21.headline: Chuppim means 'wedding canopy': neither saw the other's wedding
46:21.body: Bereshit Rabbah says Benjamin named this son חפים, Chuppim, because he did not see Joseph's wedding canopy and Joseph did not see his. It also hears 'covered over', for the lie that a wild animal had eaten Joseph.

sources.quote: וְחֻפִּים, שֶׁלֹא רָאָה בְּחֻפָּתִי וְלֹא רָאִיתִי בְּחֻפָּתוֹ, וְשֶׁחִפּוּ עָלָיו דְּבָרִים
sources.says: The midrash says Chuppim is because neither saw the other's wedding canopy, and because they covered over what had happened to him.

46:21.headline: Ard is 'a rose', or 'I will go down mourning'
46:21.body: Bereshit Rabbah gives two reasons for Benjamin's son אַרְד, Ard. Joseph was like a rose, ורד, or the name recalls Jacob's words 'I will go down to my son, mourning, to the grave'.

sources.quote: וָאָרְדְּ, שֶׁהָיָה דּוֹמֶה לְוֶרֶד. וָאָרְדְּ, עַל שֵׁם
sources.says: The midrash gives two readings of Ard: that Joseph looked like a rose, and that it recalls Jacob's 'I will go down to my son, mourning'.

46:26.headline: הבאה in verse 26 means 'coming', in verse 27 'came'
46:26.body: The same letters are stressed differently in the two verses. Rashi says the first is present tense and counts the 66 who set out from Canaan, and the second is past tense and counts the 70 who had arrived.

sources.quote: וְאֵין "הַבָּאָה" זוֹ לְשׁוֹן עָבָר אֶלָּא לְשׁוֹן הוֹוֶה
sources.says: Rashi says this הבאה is present tense, not past.

sources.quote: הַבָּאָה. מִלְעֵיל, שֶׁהוּא פֹּעַל עָבָר, וּפֵרוּשׁוֹ אֲשֶׁר בָּאָה
sources.says: Radak says the הבאה in verse 27 has its stress on the first syllable, which makes it a past verb meaning 'who came'.

sources.quote: לְפִי שֶׁכְּשֶׁיָּצְאוּ לָבֹא מֵאֶרֶץ כְּנַעַן לֹא הָיוּ אֶלָּא שִׁשִּׁים וָשֵׁשׁ
sources.says: Rashi says that when they set out to come from Canaan there were only sixty-six.

46:28.headline: 'To point the way' also hints at a house of teaching
46:28.body: Rashi says Judah went ahead to prepare a place and show them how to settle. A midrash hears 'teaching' in the word: Judah set up a house of study from which instruction would come.

sources.quote: כְּתַרְגּוּמוֹ, לְפַנּוֹת לוֹ מָקוֹם, וּלְהוֹרוֹת הֵיאַךְ יִתְיַשֵּׁב בָּהּ
sources.says: Rashi says it means to clear a place for him and to show how to settle in it.

sources.quote: וּמִדְרַשׁ אַגָּדָה לְהוֹרוֹת לְפָנָיו – לְתַקֵּן לוֹ בֵּית תַּלְמוּד שֶׁמִּשָּׁם תֵּצֵא הוֹרָאָה
sources.says: Rashi reports a midrash that it means to prepare a house of study, from which teaching would go out.

46:29.headline: Did Joseph harness his own chariot, or order it done?
46:29.body: Rashi says Joseph harnessed the horses himself, in his haste to honour his father. Ibn Ezra says it means he gave the order, as in 'Solomon built the house'.

sources.quote: הוּא עַצְמוֹ אָסַר אֶת הַסּוּסִים לַמֶּרְכָּבָה לְהִזְדָּרֵז לִכְבוֹד אָבִיו
sources.says: Rashi says Joseph himself harnessed the horses, to hurry in honour of his father.

sources.quote: על ידי צווי, כמו "ויבן שלמה את הבית"
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it was done by his command, as 'Solomon built the house' means he ordered it built.

46:29.headline: Joseph wept much more, while Jacob, the rabbis say, recited Shema
46:29.body: Rashi and Radak read עוד as 'again and again', so Joseph kept weeping. Rashi adds that Jacob did not fall on Joseph's neck, because he was saying the Shema.

sources.quote: ויבך על צואריו עוד. לְשׁוֹן הַרְבּוֹת בְּכִיָּה
sources.says: Rashi says עוד means adding more weeping.

sources.quote: אֲבָל יַעֲקֹב לֹא נָפַל עַל צַוְּארֵי יוֹסֵף וְלֹא נְשָׁקוֹ, וְאָמְרוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ, שֶׁהָיָה קוֹרֵא אֶת שְׁמַע
sources.says: Rashi says Jacob did not fall on Joseph's neck or kiss him, and the rabbis said it was because he was reciting the Shema.

sources.quote: כְּלוֹמַר פַּעַם אַחַר פַּעַם
sources.says: Radak says עוד here means 'time after time'.

46:30.headline: 'Now I can die': no fear of death, or of two deaths
46:30.body: Radak says Jacob means he no longer worries about dying now that he has seen Joseph. Rashi's midrash says Jacob had feared two deaths, in this world and the next, because God's Presence had left him over Joseph.

sources.quote: אֵינִי חוֹשֵׁשׁ שֶׁאִם אָמוּת הַפַּעַם הַזֹּאת, אַחֲרֵי רְאוֹתִי אֶת פָּנֶיךָ
sources.says: Radak says Jacob is no longer concerned if he dies this time, after seeing Joseph's face.

sources.quote: וּמִדְרָשׁוֹ סָבוּר הָיִיתִי לָמוּת שְׁתֵּי מִיתוֹת, בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה וְלָעוֹלָם הַבָּא
sources.says: Rashi gives the midrash that Jacob had thought he would die two deaths, in this world and the next.

46:34.headline: Why were shepherds hated in Egypt? Sheep were sacred there
46:34.body: Rashi and Maimonides say the Egyptians treated the sheep as sacred, so they loathed those who herd it. Ibn Ezra says Egyptians then did not eat meat at all.

sources.quote: כי תועבת מצרים כל רועה צאן. לְפִי שֶׁהֵם לָהֶם אֱלֹהוּת
sources.says: Rashi says shepherds were an abomination because the sheep were gods to them.

sources.quote: התורה כבר אמרה במפורש, כמו שפירש אנקלוס, שהמצרים הקדמונים היו עובדים את מזל טלה
sources.says: Maimonides says that, as Onkelos explained, the ancient Egyptians worshipped the sign of the ram.

sources.quote: לאות כי בימים ההם לא הי' המצרים אוכלים בשר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says that in those days the Egyptians did not eat meat.

47:2.headline: 'From the end of his brothers': the five weakest, or the greatest?
47:2.body: Radak says the sages disagree whether Joseph took the five weakest brothers or the five greatest. Rashi follows those who say the weakest, so Pharaoh would not make them soldiers.

sources.quote: לָקַח מֵהֶם חֲמִשָּׁה הַפְּחוּתִים מֵהֶם אוֹ הַגְּדוֹלִים מֵהֶם
sources.says: Radak says Joseph took five of them, either the lowest or the greatest, and that the sages disagree.

sources.quote: מִן הַפְּחוּתִים שֶׁבָּהֶם לִגְבוּרָה, שֶׁאֵין נִרְאִים גִּבּוֹרִים
sources.says: Rashi says Joseph took the weakest in strength, who did not look like warriors.

sources.quote: מִפְּנֵי מָה אָמַר הַכָּתוּב וּמִקְצֵה אֶחָיו, לְלַמֶּדְךָ שֶׁלֹא הָיוּ גִבּוֹרִים
sources.says: The midrash says the verse says 'from the end of his brothers' to teach that these were not mighty men.

47:6.headline: 'Men of חיל' means skilled with flocks, or fit for power
47:6.body: חיל is often 'strength' or 'army'. Rashi and Radak say here it means skilled at tending livestock, while Rashbam says it means fit for strength and rank, as in 'woman of חיל'.

sources.quote: בְּקִיאִין בְּאֻמָּנוּתָן לִרְעוֹת צֹאן
sources.says: Rashi says it means expert in their trade of tending sheep.

sources.quote: אַנְשֵׁי־חַיִל. בְּעִנְיַן הַמִּקְנֶה
sources.says: Radak says it means men of חיל in matters of livestock.

sources.quote: ראויים לגבורה ולשררה כמו: אשת חיל את
sources.says: Rashbam says it means fit for strength and authority, like 'a woman of חיל'.

47:7.headline: Did Jacob 'bless' Pharaoh, or just greet him?
47:7.body: Rashi says ויברך here is a greeting, as people who appear before kings do. Ramban disagrees: it was a real blessing, as elders and pious men bless a king with wealth and honour.

sources.quote: הִיא שְׁאִילַת שָׁלוֹם כְּדֶרֶךְ כָּל הַנִּרְאִים לִפְנֵי הַמְּלָכִים לִפְרָקִים
sources.says: Rashi says it is a greeting, the way people who appear before kings from time to time do.

sources.quote: אֲבָל הָיָה בְּרָכָה מַמָּשׁ, שֶׁדֶּרֶךְ הַזְּקֵנִים וְהַחֲסִידִים הַבָּאִים לִפְנֵי הַמְּלָכִים לְבָרֵךְ אוֹתָם בְּעֹשֶׁר וּנְכָסִים וְכָבוֹד
sources.says: Ramban says it was a real blessing, as elders and pious men bless kings with wealth, property and honour.

47:9.headline: Why does a man of 130 call his years 'few'?
47:9.body: Ramban says Pharaoh was amazed at how old Jacob looked, so Jacob answered that his years were few next to his fathers', but hard. Radak says Jacob felt his weakness and knew he had little time left.

sources.quote: וְנִרְאֶה לִי כִּי יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ זָרְקָה בּוֹ שֵׂיבָה וְהָיָה נִרְאֶה זָקֵן מְאֹד
sources.says: Ramban says Jacob had gone grey from hardship and looked very old, which is why Pharaoh asked his age.

sources.quote: לפי שנראה יעקב בעיניו זקן יותר מדאי
sources.says: Rashbam says Jacob looked too old to Pharaoh, so Jacob explained that his years were few but hard.

sources.quote: אֶלָּא מִפְּנֵי הַצָּרוֹת שֶׁמְּצָאוּהוּ הִרְגִּישׁ בְּעַצְמוֹ חָלְשׁוֹ
sources.says: Radak says that because of his troubles Jacob felt his own weakness, and knew he could live only a little longer.

47:10.headline: Jacob's parting blessing: that the Nile would rise at Pharaoh's feet
47:10.body: Rashi says people leaving a ruler bless him and take leave. He says Jacob's blessing was that the Nile would rise to meet Pharaoh, since Egypt is watered by the Nile and not by rain.

sources.quote: וּמַה בְּרָכָה בֵּרְכוֹ? שֶׁיַּעֲלֶה נִילוּס לְרַגְלָיו
sources.says: Rashi asks what the blessing was, and answers that the Nile would rise at his feet.

47:13.headline: ותלה: the land grew weary, or went mad with hunger
47:13.body: This form appears only here. Rashi reads it as 'grew weary', Radak as madness since hunger drives people mad, and Ibn Ezra as being like someone who does not know what to do.

sources.quote: ותלה. כְּמוֹ וַתִּלְאֶה, לְשׁוֹן עֲיֵפוּת, כְּתַרְגּוּמוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says it is like 'grew weary', a word of exhaustion, as Onkelos translates it.

sources.quote: וַתֵּלַהּ. עִנְיַן שִׁגָּעוֹן, כִּי מִפְּנֵי הָרָעָב יִשְׁתַּגַּע הָאָדָם
sources.says: Radak says it means madness, because hunger can drive a person mad.

sources.quote: וטעמו כאדם שלא ידע מה יעשה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means like a person who does not know what to do.

47:15.headline: אפס usually means 'nothing', but here it is a verb: 'ran out'
47:15.body: The people say 'the money אפס'. Rashi, following Onkelos, says it means the money was finished, and Ibn Ezra says it is a past-tense verb.

sources.quote: אפס. כְּתַרְגּוּמוֹ שְׁלִים
sources.says: Rashi says אפס means 'finished', as Onkelos translates it.

sources.quote: אפס כסף. פועל עבר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says אפס כסף is a past-tense verb.

47:17.headline: וינהלם: Joseph 'led' them with bread, or fed them slowly
47:17.body: Rashi says it is like 'led them', and compares 'He leads me beside still waters'. Sforno says it means Joseph fed them gently, a little at a time, as is right in a famine.

sources.quote: וינהלם. כְּמוֹ וַיְנַהֲגֵם
sources.says: Rashi says וינהלם means the same as 'he led them'.

sources.quote: נָתַן לָהֶם הַלֶּחֶם מְעַט מְעַט, אָכוֹל וְלֹא לְשָׂבְעָה
sources.says: Sforno says Joseph gave them the bread a little at a time, enough to eat but not to be full.

47:21.headline: Why did Joseph move the people from city to city?
47:21.body: The verse does not say why Joseph moved the people. Rashi says it was to spare his brothers the shame of being called exiles, when everyone had been moved, and Rashbam says it stopped people claiming their old fields.

sources.quote: שֶׁנִּתְכַּוֵּן לְהָסִיר חֶרְפָּה מֵעַל אֶחָיו, שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיוּ קוֹרִין אוֹתָם גּוֹלִים
sources.says: Rashi says Joseph meant to remove shame from his brothers, so that they would not be called exiles.

sources.quote: כדי שלא יטענו בה חזקה איש איש בארצו לאחר מכירה
sources.says: Rashbam says it was so that no one could claim a hold on his own land after the sale.

47:22.headline: Egypt's 'כהנים': idol priests, or princes?
47:22.body: Rashi and Radak say these were priests of idols. Chizkuni says they were officials, like the 'כהן of Midian'.

sources.quote: הַכּוּמָרִים, כָּל לְשׁוֹן כֹּהֵן מְשָׁרֵת לֶאֱלֹהוּת הוּא, חוּץ מֵאוֹתָן שֶׁהֵם לְשׁוֹן גְּדֻלָּה, כְּמוֹ כֹּהֵן מִדְיָן, כֹּהֵן אוֹן
sources.says: Rashi says כהנים here means idol priests; כהן always means one who serves a god, except where it means greatness, as with the כהן of Midian or On.

sources.quote: הַכֹּהֲנִים, כּוֹמְרֵי הַבָּמוֹת
sources.says: Radak says the כהנים were the priests of the high places.

sources.quote: רק אדמת הכהנים השרים כמו כהן מדין
sources.says: Chizkuni says the כהנים were princes, like the כהן of Midian.

47:22.headline: חק means a bread ration here, a law in verse 26
47:22.body: Rashi says the priests' חק is a fixed amount of bread per day. In verse 26 the same word means a standing law, one that was not to be crossed.

sources.quote: חֹק כָּךְ וְכָךְ לֶחֶם לַיּוֹם
sources.says: Rashi says the חק was such and such an amount of bread per day.

sources.quote: לחק. שֶׁלֹּא יַעֲבֹר
sources.says: Rashi says לחק means a law that will not be crossed.

47:28.headline: Why there is no gap before 'And Jacob lived'
47:28.body: The section is closed, with no gap. Rashi says it is because when Jacob died, Israel's eyes and hearts were closed by the pain of slavery, and Chizkuni says Jacob truly 'lived' only in Egypt, since his earlier life was in distress.

sources.quote: לָמָּה פָּרָשָׁה זוֹ סְתוּמָה? לְפִי שֶׁכֵּיוָן שֶׁנִּפְטַר יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ נִסְתְּמוּ עֵינֵיהֶם וְלִבָּם שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל מִצָּרַת הַשִּׁעְבּוּד
sources.says: Rashi says the section is closed because once Jacob died, Israel's eyes and hearts were shut by the distress of slavery.

sources.quote: ויחי יעקב בארץ מצרים אבל כל שאר שנותיו וחייו לא היו חיים שכל ימיו היה שרוי בצער
sources.says: Chizkuni says Jacob 'lived' in Egypt, but the rest of his years were not really life, since he was in distress all his days.

47:29.headline: 'Drew near to dying' is a special phrase with a pattern
47:29.body: Rashi says everyone this phrase is used of died younger than their fathers. Rashbam says it marks a person about to give final instructions to his sons.

sources.quote: כָּל מִי שֶׁנֶּאֱמְרָה בּוֹ קְרִיבָה לָמוּת, לֹא הִגִּיעַ לִימֵי אֲבוֹתָיו
sources.says: Rashi says everyone of whom 'drew near to dying' is said did not reach the years of his fathers.

sources.quote: כל מקום שאדם חפץ לצוות את בניו צריך לאמר ויקרבו
sources.says: Rashbam says wherever a person wants to command his sons, the text says 'they drew near'.

47:29.headline: 'Kindness and truth': why burial is called a kindness of truth
47:29.body: Jacob asks for 'kindness and truth'. Rashi says kindness to the dead is true kindness because the dead cannot repay, while Radak splits the words: truth is the duty to bury your father, kindness is carrying him back to Canaan.

sources.quote: חֶסֶד שֶׁעוֹשִׂין עִם הַמֵּתִים הוּא חֶסֶד שֶׁל אֱמֶת, שֶׁאֵינוֹ מְצַפֶּה לְתַשְׁלוּם גְּמוּל
sources.says: Rashi says kindness done for the dead is true kindness, since one expects no repayment.

sources.quote: הָאֱמֶת הוּא שֶׁחַיָּב לִקְבֹּר אֶת אָבִיו, וְהַחֶסֶד הוּא שֶׁיִּשָּׂאוּהוּ מִמִּצְרַיִם
sources.says: Radak says the truth is that Joseph must bury his father, and the kindness is that he carry him out of Egypt.

47:30.headline: 'I will lie with my fathers' means dying, not being buried
47:30.body: Rashi says 'lying with his fathers' always means dying, not burial, so it cannot mean 'lay me in the cave'. Ibn Ezra says it is a way of saying death, or else it means that he will be buried with them.

sources.quote: מָצִינוּ בְּכָל מָקוֹם לְשׁוֹן שְׁכִיבָה עִם אֲבוֹתָיו הִיא הַגְּוִיעָה וְלֹא הַקְּבוּרָה
sources.says: Rashi says 'lying with his fathers' everywhere means the dying and not the burial.

sources.quote: כנוי למיתה, או יהיה פירושו אל נא תקברני במצרים ואשכב עם אבותי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is a figure for death, or else means: do not bury me in Egypt, so that I may lie with my fathers.

47:31.headline: Whom did Jacob bow to: Joseph, the crown, or God?
47:31.body: Rashbam says Jacob bowed to Joseph. Ibn Ezra says it was respect to the crown, or more likely praise to God, and Radak says he thanked and bowed to God.

sources.quote: וישתחו ישראל - ליוסף
sources.says: Rashbam says Jacob bowed to Joseph.

sources.quote: שחלק כבוד למלכות, והנכון בעיני שנתן שבח שם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says one view is that he honoured the monarchy, but he thinks the right view is that he gave praise to God.

sources.quote: וַיִּשְׁתַּחוּ. הוֹדָה וְהִשְׁתַּחֲוָה לָאֵל
sources.says: Radak says Jacob gave thanks and bowed to God.

47:31.headline: 'Head of the bed' also hints that his family line was whole
47:31.body: Rashi says Jacob turned toward the Divine Presence, which rests above a sick person's head. A second reading says 'bed' means his descendants: none of them was wicked.

sources.quote: הָפַךְ עַצְמוֹ לְצַד הַשְּׁכִינָה. מִכָּאן אָמְרוּ שֶׁהַשְּׁכִינָה לְמַעְלָה מֵרַאֲשׁוֹתָיו שֶׁל חוֹלֶה
sources.says: Rashi says Jacob turned toward the Divine Presence, which sits above the head of a sick person.

sources.quote: עַל רֹאשׁ הַמִּטָּה – עַל שֶׁהָיְתָה מִטָּתוֹ שְׁלֵמָה וְלֹא הָיָה בָהּ רֶשַׁע
sources.says: Rashi gives another reading: because his bed was whole and had no wickedness in it.

48:2.headline: Why Jacob 'strengthened himself' when Joseph came
48:2.body: Rashi says Jacob thought: he is my son, but he is a king, so I will honour him. From this Rashi learns that we give honour to royalty.

sources.quote: אָמַר, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהוּא בְּנִי, מֶלֶךְ הוּא, אֶחֱלֹק לוֹ כָּבוֹד
sources.says: Rashi says Jacob said: although he is my son, he is a king, so I will give him honour.

48:4.headline: 'A company of nations': Rashi hears a promise of one more tribe
48:4.body: Rashi says God told Jacob that another assembly of peoples would come from him. No son was born after Benjamin, so Jacob understood that one of his sons' tribes would be split in two, and now he gives that gift to Joseph.

sources.quote: בִּשְּׂרַנִי שֶׁעֲתִידִים לָצֵאת מִמֶּנִּי עוֹד קָהָל וְעַמִּים
sources.says: Rashi says God announced that yet another assembly and peoples would come from Jacob.

48:7.headline: כברת ארץ is a rare measure: 2,000 cubits, or a day's ploughing
48:7.body: The phrase appears only a few times. Rashi says it is a measure of land of 2,000 cubits, as with the Sabbath limit, and that Onkelos renders it as the length a person ploughs in a day.

sources.quote: כברת ארץ. מִדַּת אֶרֶץ, וְהֵם אַלְפַּיִם אַמָּה כְּמִדַּת תְּחוּם שַׁבָּת
sources.says: Rashi says כברת ארץ is a measure of land, 2,000 cubits, like the Sabbath boundary.

sources.quote: וְאֻנְקְלוֹס תִּרְגֵּם כְּרוּב אַרְעָא – כְּדֵי שִׁעוּר חֲרִישַׁת יוֹם
sources.says: Rashi says Onkelos translated it as about the distance of a day's ploughing.

48:7.headline: Why did Jacob bury Rachel on the road?
48:7.body: Jacob tells Joseph he buried Rachel there. Ibn Ezra says she died suddenly and he could not carry her to the cave, while Rashi says it was by God's command, so that she could weep for her children when they were exiled.

sources.quote: שמתה פתאום, ולא יכולתי להוליכה לקברה במערה כאשר קברתי לאה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says she died suddenly and Jacob could not take her to the cave, as he had Leah.

sources.quote: עַל פִּי הַדִּבּוּר קְבַרְתִּיהָ שָׁם, שֶׁתְּהֵא לְעֶזְרָה לְבָנֶיהָ כְּשֶׁיַּגְלֶה אוֹתָם נְבוּזַרְאֲדָן
sources.says: Rashi says Jacob buried her there by God's word, so she would help her children when Nebuzaradan exiled them.

48:9.headline: What does בזה mean: this place, this kingdom, or a contract?
48:9.body: Joseph says God gave him these sons 'בזה'. Radak says it means 'in this place', Rashbam says 'in this kingdom', and Rashi says Joseph showed his father the betrothal and marriage contracts.

sources.quote: הֶרְאָה לוֹ שְׁטָר אֵרוּסִין וּשְׁטָר כְּתֻבָּה
sources.says: Rashi says Joseph showed him the betrothal document and the marriage contract.

sources.quote: בַּמָּקוֹם הַזֶּה, וְכֵן (בראשית לח:כא) ״לֹא הָיְתָה בָזֶה קְדֵשָׁה״
sources.says: Radak says it means 'in this place', as in 'there was no harlot in this place'.

sources.quote: במלכות הזאת
sources.says: Rashbam says it means 'in this kingdom'.

48:11.headline: פללתי: 'I never thought', 'I never judged', or 'I never prayed'?
48:11.body: Jacob says he never פללתי to see Joseph's face. Rashi says the word means thought, and Radak says it can mean judged or, as some say, prayed, since he had given up hope.

sources.quote: פללתי לְשׁוֹן מַחֲשָׁבָה, כְּמוֹ הָבִיאִי עֵצָה עֲשׂוּ פְלִילָה
sources.says: Rashi says פללתי means thought, as in 'bring counsel, make a decision' in Isaiah.

sources.quote: כְּלוֹמַר לֹא דַנְתִּי בְּעַצְמִי וְלֹא חָשַׁבְתִּי שֶׁאֶרְאֲךָ עוֹד
sources.says: Radak says it means I did not judge in myself, I did not think I would see you again.

sources.quote: וְיֵשׁ מְפָרְשִׁים (מדרש לקח טוב בראשית מח:יא) פִלָּלְתִּי עִנְיַן תְּפִלָּה
sources.says: Radak reports that some explain פללתי as prayer, because Jacob thought he would pray in vain.

48:14.headline: שכל את ידיו: Jacob guided his hands wisely, or crossed them
48:14.body: This form appears only here. Rashi, Radak and Ibn Ezra link it to wisdom, as if Jacob guided his hands with understanding, while Rashbam links it to a word for twisted, since Jacob crossed his hands.

sources.quote: בְּהַשְׂכֵּל וְחָכְמָה הִשְׂכִּיל אֶת יָדָיו לְכָךְ וּמִדַּעַת
sources.says: Rashi says Jacob guided his hands with wisdom and knowledge.

sources.quote: כְּלוֹמַר נָתַן שֵׂכֶל לְיָדָיו, כְּאִלּוּ עָשָׂה בְּשֵׂכֶל וּבְחָכְמָה מַה שֶּׁעָשָׂה
sources.says: Radak says he gave his hands understanding, as if he acted with sense and wisdom.

sources.quote: כאילו ידיו השכילו מה שהוא רוצה לעשות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is as if his hands understood what he wanted to do.

sources.quote: כמו שכל שהוא לשון אדם מעוקם ונפתל
sources.says: Rashbam says it is like a word that means a person who is bent and twisted.

48:16.headline: 'The angel who redeems me': who is the angel?
48:16.body: Jacob blesses with 'the angel' right after naming God. Rashi says it is the angel who was regularly sent to him in his troubles, and Radak says God acts through messengers, which is why the angel is named next.

sources.quote: מַלְאָךְ הָרָגִיל לְהִשְׁתַּלֵּחַ אֵלַי בְּצָרָתִי
sources.says: Rashi says it is the angel who is used to being sent to me in my trouble.

sources.quote: לְפִי שֶׁמַּעֲשֵׂה הָאֵל הוּא עַל יְדֵי אֶמְצָעִים וְהַמַּלְאָכִים הֵם שְׁלוּחִים מֵהָאֵל לַעֲבָדָיו
sources.says: Radak says God's actions are carried out through means, and angels are God's messengers to His servants.

48:16.headline: 'Let them grow like fish': a blessing from the word for fish
48:16.body: The verb is built on דג, fish. Rashi says it is a blessing to be fruitful like fish, over which the evil eye has no power, and Radak says it means they will multiply like fish.

sources.quote: כַּדָּגִים הַלָּלוּ שֶׁפָּרִים וְרָבִים וְאֵין עַיִן הָרָע שׁוֹלֶטֶת בָּהֶם
sources.says: Rashi says like these fish, which are fruitful and multiply, and over which the evil eye has no power.

sources.quote: וְיִדְגּוּ לָרֹב. יִרְבּוּ כְּמוֹ הַדָּגִים
sources.says: Radak says וידגו means they will multiply like the fish.

48:19.headline: 'The younger will be greater': greater in numbers, or in rank?
48:19.body: Radak says יגדל here means rank and honour, since Ephraim gave leaders such as Joshua and the first king of the northern tribes. Rashi points to Joshua, who taught Israel Torah and gave them the land.

sources.quote: אִם כֵּן יִגְדַּל רוֹצֶה לוֹמַר לְשׁוֹן גְּדֻלָּה וְרוֹמְמוּת
sources.says: Radak says יגדל means greatness and exaltation, not numbers.

sources.quote: שֶׁעָתִיד יְהוֹשֻׁעַ לָצֵאת מִמֶּנּוּ, שֶׁיַּנְחִיל אֶת הָאָרֶץ וִילַמֵּד תּוֹרָה לְיִשְׂרָאֵל
sources.says: Rashi says Joshua would come from him, who would give Israel the land and teach them Torah.

48:19.headline: 'Full of nations': a famous name, exile, or many nations
48:19.body: Rashi says the world will fill with Joshua's fame when he stops the sun. Radak says Ephraim's children will fill the lands of the nations in exile, and Ibn Ezra says many nations will come from him.

sources.quote: כָּל הָעוֹלָם יִתְמַלֵּא בְּצֵאת שָׁמְעוֹ וּשְׁמוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says the whole world will be filled when his fame and name go out.

sources.quote: בְּגָלוּתוֹ בֵּינֵיהֶם שֶׁיְּמַלְּאוּ אַרְצוֹת הַגּוֹיִם מֵהֶם
sources.says: Radak says it means that in their exile among the nations, they will fill the nations' lands.

sources.quote: גוים רבים יצאו ממנו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says many nations will come out from him.

48:20.headline: Jacob 'put' Ephraim first: in the blessing's words, and in rank
48:20.body: Ibn Ezra and Rashbam say Jacob put Ephraim first in the words of the blessing, 'like Ephraim and like Manasseh'. Rashi says it also gave Ephraim the lead in the camp banners and the princes' offerings.

sources.quote: באומרו - ישימך אלהים כאפרים וכמנשה - וכן לשון שימה נופל בדברים
sources.says: Rashbam says Jacob placed Ephraim first by saying 'like Ephraim and like Manasseh', and that 'placing' can be said of words.

sources.quote: וישם את אפרים. בדבור הברכה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the placing was in the words of the blessing.

sources.quote: בְּבִרְכָתוֹ לִפְנֵי מְנַשֶּׁה, לְהַקְדִּימוֹ בִּדְגָלִים וּבַחֲנֻכַּת הַנְּשִׂיאִים
sources.says: Rashi says he put Ephraim before Manasseh in his blessing, to put him first in the banners and the dedication offerings of the princes.

48:22.headline: 'One Shechem': the city, or one extra portion
48:22.body: Jacob gives Joseph 'Shechem one'. Rashi says it is the city, where Joseph was later buried, or else a portion, meaning the firstborn's extra share, and Bereshit Rabbah also hears 'rose early' in the name.

sources.quote: שְׁכֶם מַמָּשׁ, הִיא תִּהְיֶה לְךָ חֵלֶק אֶחָד יְתֵרָה עַל אַחֶיךָ
sources.says: Rashi says it is the actual city of Shechem, which will be an extra portion for Joseph beyond his brothers.

sources.quote: דָּבָר אַחֵר שְׁכֶם אַחַד הוּא הַבְּכוֹרָה, שֶׁיִּטְּלוּ בָנָיו שְׁנֵי חֲלָקִים, וּשְׁכֶם לְשׁוֹן חֵלֶק הוּא
sources.says: Rashi gives another reading: 'one Shechem' is the birthright, two portions for his sons, since שכם means a portion.

sources.quote: והנכון בעיני שפי' שכם אחד חלק אחד
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says he thinks the right reading is 'one portion'.

sources.quote: בֵּן שֶׁהִשְׁכִּים וְלֹא עָשִׂיתָ כְּמַעֲשֵׂיהֶן, לְפִיכָךְ תְּהֵא הַשְּׁכֶם בְּחֶלְקֶךָ
sources.says: The midrash says: a son who rose early and did not act as they did, therefore Shechem will be in your portion.

48:22.headline: 'With my sword and my bow': real weapons, or prayer?
48:22.body: Rashi says Jacob girded for battle when Simeon and Levi killed the men of Shechem, and also that the sword and bow are his wisdom and prayer. Ibn Ezra says they stand for God, as David called God 'my shield'.

sources.quote: כְּשֶׁהָרְגוּ שִׁמְעוֹן וְלֵוִי אֶת אַנְשֵׁי שְׁכֶם נִתְכַּנְּסוּ כָּל סְבִיבוֹתֵיהֶם לְהִזְדַּוֵּג לָהֶם, וְחָגַר יַעֲקֹב כְּלֵי מִלְחָמָה כְּנֶגְדָּן
sources.says: Rashi says that when Simeon and Levi killed Shechem's men, their neighbours gathered, and Jacob girded for war against them.

sources.quote: בחרבי ובקשתי. הִיא חָכְמָתוֹ וּתְפִלָּתוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says 'my sword and my bow' are his wisdom and his prayer.

sources.quote: וטעם בחרבי ובקשתי על השם כאשר אמר דוד
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says 'my sword and bow' refers to God, as David spoke of Him.

48:22.headline: 'From the Amorite': Esau's deeds, or his hunting with words
48:22.body: Rashi says the Amorite is Esau, who acted as an Amorite, or else it hears אמרי as 'words': Esau hunted his father with the words of his mouth. Ibn Ezra says the Amorites are named because they were the strongest of the seven nations.

sources.quote: מִיַּד עֵשָׂו, שֶׁעָשָׂה מַעֲשֵׂה אֱמוֹרִי. דָּבָר אַחֵר שֶׁהָיָה צָד אָבִיו בְּאִמְרֵי פִיו
sources.says: Rashi says it means from Esau's hand, who acted like an Amorite, or, another reading, because he hunted his father with the words of his mouth.

sources.quote: והזכיר האמורי בעבור שאין בשבעה גוים חזק כמוהו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the Amorite is named because none of the seven nations was as strong.

49:1.headline: Jacob tried to reveal the end of days, and God's Presence left
49:1.body: Rashi says Jacob tried to tell his sons when the end would come, the Divine Presence left him, and he spoke of other things. Ibn Ezra says these words are prophecy of what will happen to each tribe, not just blessings.

sources.quote: בִּקֵּשׁ לְגַלּוֹת אֶת הַקֵּץ וְנִסְתַּלְּקָה מִמֶּנּוּ שְׁכִינָה וְהִתְחִיל אוֹמֵר דְּבָרִים אַחֵרִים
sources.says: Rashi says Jacob wanted to reveal the end, the Divine Presence left him, and he began to say other things.

sources.quote: דבר הנביא לעתיד, ותעו האומרים שהם ברכות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says this is the prophet speaking of the future, and those who say these are blessings are mistaken.

49:3.headline: אוני can mean strength, a first seed, or wealth
49:3.body: Reuben is called 'the first of my אוני'. Rashi says אוני means strength, and here it is the first drop of seed, since Jacob had never wasted seed before, while Rashbam says it is wealth, as in 'I have found אוֹן for myself'.

sources.quote: הִיא טִפָּה רִאשׁוֹנָה, שֶׁלֹּא רָאָה קֶרִי מִיָּמָיו
sources.says: Rashi says it is the first drop, since Jacob had never had an emission in all his days.

sources.quote: אוני. כּוֹחִי, כְּמוֹ מָצָאתִי אוֹן לִי
sources.says: Rashi says אוני means my strength, as in 'I have found אוֹן for myself'.

sources.quote: וגם אוני ממוני הוא, כדכתיב: מצאתי און לי
sources.says: Rashbam says אוני also means my wealth, as in 'I have found אוֹן for myself'.

49:3.headline: 'Excess of שאת, excess of עז': priesthood and kingship
49:3.body: Rashi says שאת means the raising of hands, the priesthood, and עז means kingship, and that Reuben as firstborn should have had both. Rashbam also reads עז as ruling over his brothers.

sources.quote: רָאוּי הָיִיתָ לִהְיוֹת יֶתֶר עַל אַחֶיךָ בִכְהֻנָּה, לְשׁוֹן נְשִׂיאוּת כַּפַּיִם
sources.says: Rashi says Reuben deserved to be above his brothers in the priesthood, from the lifting of hands.

sources.quote: ויתר עז. בְּמַלְכוּת, כְּמוֹ: וְיִתֶּן עֹז לְמַלְכּוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says עז here means kingship, as in 'He gives strength to His king'.

sources.quote: ויתר עז היה לך למלוך על אחיך
sources.says: Rashbam says Reuben should have had the excess of ruling over his brothers.

49:4.headline: פחז, a word found only here, means hasty and rushing like water
49:4.body: Reuben is likened to water that rushes. Rashi says it means a hasty, hurried show of anger, and Ibn Ezra links it to a word for reckless men in Judges.

sources.quote: הַפַּחַז וְהַבֶּהָלָה אֲשֶׁר מִהַרְתָּ לְהַרְאוֹת כַּעַסְךָ כַּמַּיִם הַלָּלוּ הַמְמַהֲרִים לִמְרוּצָתָם
sources.says: Rashi says it is the haste and hurry with which Reuben rushed to show his anger, like water rushing on its way.

sources.quote: ופחז מגזרת אנשים רקים ופוחזים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says פחז comes from the same root as 'empty and reckless men' in Judges.

49:4.headline: 'You shall not excel': Reuben loses his extra share
49:4.body: Rashi says אל תותר means do not take all the extra shares that were yours. Ibn Ezra gives two readings: you will have no advantage, or, as others say, you were like poured-out water and nothing was left.

sources.quote: אַל תַּרְבֶּה לִטֹּל כָּל הַיְתֵרוֹת הַלָּלוּ שֶׁהָיוּ רְאוּיוֹת לְךָ
sources.says: Rashi says do not take all those extra shares that were due to you.

sources.quote: אל תותר. לא יהיה לך יתרון
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means you will have no advantage.

sources.quote: ואחרים אמרו רק אתה פחזת כמים הנשפכים ולא הותרת כלום
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports others who say that you rushed like poured-out water and nothing was left.

49:5.headline: 'Simeon and Levi are brothers': brothers in what?
49:5.body: Rashi says they were 'brothers' in a shared plan against both Shechem and Joseph. Ibn Ezra says it is only about the affair of Shechem.

sources.quote: עַל כָּרְחֲךָ שִׁמְעוֹן וְלֵוִי הֵם שֶׁקְּרָאָם אֲבִיהֶם אַחִים
sources.says: Rashi says it must be Simeon and Levi whom their father called 'brothers', in one counsel against Shechem and Joseph.

sources.quote: שמעון ולוי אחים. בעבור מעשה שכם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says they are called brothers because of the affair at Shechem.

49:5.headline: 'Tools of violence': murder was Esau's craft
49:5.body: Rashi says murder was a trade Simeon and Levi took from Esau. He ties it to Isaac's blessing of Esau, 'by your sword you shall live'.

sources.quote: אֻמָּנוּת זוֹ שֶׁל רְצִיחָה, חָמָס הוּא בִידֵיהֶם – מִבִּרְכַּת עֵשָׂו הִיא זוֹ, אֻמָּנוּת שֶׁלּוֹ הִיא
sources.says: Rashi says this trade of killing is violence in their hands; it comes from Esau's blessing and is his craft.

49:5.headline: מכרתיהם is found only here, and several readings are offered
49:5.body: Rashi says it is a word for swords, which he says sounds like the Greek, or, as Onkelos has it, the land of their dwelling. Ibn Ezra prefers a link to 'your origin' in Ezekiel, and Rashbam says it means their brotherhood.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן כְּלֵי זַיִן, הַסַּיִף בִּלְשׁוֹן יְוָנִי
sources.says: Rashi says it means weapons, and that 'sword' in Greek sounds like it.

sources.quote: בְּאֶרֶץ מְגוּרָתָם נָהֲגוּ עַצְמָן בִּכְלֵי חָמָס
sources.says: Rashi gives a second reading, as Onkelos translates: in the land of their dwelling they acted with tools of violence.

sources.quote: והנכון בעיני שהוא מגזרת "מְכרֹותַיִךְ"
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says he thinks it comes from the same root as 'your origin' in Ezekiel.

sources.quote: אַחֲוֹתֵיהֶם כפל לשון של שמעון ולוי אחים
sources.says: Rashbam says it means their brotherhood, repeating 'Simeon and Levi are brothers'.

49:6.headline: 'Let me not enter their council': the council of Zimri
49:6.body: Rashi says the 'council' is the plot of Zimri, when Simeon's tribe gathered about the Midianite woman. Jacob asks that his name not be linked with it.

sources.quote: זֶה מַעֲשֵׂה זִמְרִי, כְּשֶׁנִּתְקַבְּצוּ שִׁבְטוֹ שֶׁל שִׁמְעוֹן
sources.says: Rashi says this is the affair of Zimri, when Simeon's tribe gathered.

sources.quote: וטעם בסודם כמו "בהוסדם יחד עלי"
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says בסודם means as in 'when they took counsel together against me'.

49:6.headline: תחד is rare: let Jacob's name not be joined to theirs
49:6.body: Rashi says it means 'be joined', so that Jacob's name is not tied to theirs. He notes that Korach's family line stops at Levi, not Jacob.

sources.quote: אַל יִתְיַחֵד עִמָּהֶם שְׁמִי, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר קֹרַח בֶּן יִצְהָר בֶּן קְהָת בֶּן לֵוִי, וְלֹא נֶאֱמַר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב
sources.says: Rashi says: let my name not be united with theirs, since the verse says Korach son of Levi, and not son of Jacob.

sources.quote: תחד. מלשון יחד
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says תחד comes from the word for 'together'.

49:6.headline: 'My honour' means Jacob himself, speaking to his own soul
49:6.body: Rashi says כבודי must be read as Jacob speaking to his own honour, telling it not to join them. Ibn Ezra, quoting another scholar, says 'my honour' is the same as 'my soul'.

sources.quote: כָּבוֹד לְשׁוֹן זָכָר הוּא, וְעַל כָּרְחֲךָ אַתָּה צָרִיךְ לְפָרֵשׁ כִּמְדַבֵּר אֶל הַכָּבוֹד
sources.says: Rashi says כבוד is masculine, so it must be read as Jacob speaking to his own honour.

sources.quote: כי כבודי כמו נפשי, ורבים בס' תהלות כמוהו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says 'my honour' is like 'my soul', as in many verses in Psalms.

49:6.headline: 'They killed an איש': one man, or many men?
49:6.body: Rashi's midrash says the 'man' is Hamor and the people of Shechem, who counted as one man, and on the plain reading he says איש stands for many men. Ibn Ezra says it is a type, like 'ox and donkey'.

sources.quote: אֵלּוּ חֲמוֹר וְאַנְשֵׁי שְׁכֶם, וְאֵינָן חֲשׁוּבִין כֻּלָּם אֶלָּא כְאִישׁ אֶחָד
sources.says: Rashi says these are Hamor and the men of Shechem, all counted only as one man.

sources.quote: אֲנָשִׁים הַרְבֵּה קוֹרֵא אִישׁ – כָּל אֶחָד לְעַצְמוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says on the plain reading the verse calls many people 'a man', each one on his own.

sources.quote: הרגו איש. שם המין, כמו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says איש is the name of a kind, like 'ox and donkey', and points to the men of Shechem.

49:6.headline: עקרו is to cut the legs from under, as with horses
49:6.body: Rashi and Rashbam link עקרו to 'you shall hamstring their horses' in Joshua. Rashi adds that the 'ox' they wanted to uproot is Joseph.

sources.quote: עִקְּרוּ אשרי"טיר בְּלַעַז, לְשׁוֹן אֶת סוּסֵיהֶם תְּעַקֵּר
sources.says: Rashi says עקרו is 'to tear out' in old French, like 'you shall hamstring their horses'.

sources.quote: עקרו שור - כמו: ואת סוסיהם תעקר
sources.says: Rashbam says עקרו is like 'you shall hamstring their horses'.

49:6.headline: 'They hamstrung an ox': Joseph, or the walled city?
49:6.body: Rashi says the 'ox' is Joseph, who is called an ox elsewhere. Ibn Ezra says שור means a wall, as in verse 22, and points to the walled city of Shechem.

sources.quote: רָצוּ לַעֲקֹר אֶת יוֹסֵף שֶׁנִּקְרָא שׁוֹר
sources.says: Rashi says they wanted to uproot Joseph, who is called 'ox'.

sources.quote: שור. חומה, וכן "צעדה עלי שור"
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says שור means a wall, as in 'a branch over a wall' in verse 22.

49:7.headline: 'Cursed be their anger': only the anger was cursed
49:7.body: Rashi says that even in rebuke Jacob cursed only their anger, not them. Ibn Ezra says it is prophecy or a prayer that their anger would fade, since 'cursed' is the opposite of 'blessed'.

sources.quote: אֲפִלּוּ בִּשְׁעַת תּוֹכֵחָה לֹא קִלֵּל אֶלָּא אַפָּם
sources.says: Rashi says even at the moment of rebuke Jacob cursed only their anger.

sources.quote: דרך נבואה או דרך תפלה, שיחסר אפם וטוב להם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is a prophecy or a prayer that their anger would lessen, and it would be good for them.

49:7.headline: 'I will divide them': Simeon scattered, Levi spread among the tribes
49:7.body: Rashi says the scattering was real: Levi was set apart from the tribal count, and Simeon produced the poor, scribes and teachers who wander. Ibn Ezra notes Simeon's land lay inside Judah's, and Levi's cities were spread among the tribes.

sources.quote: אֵין לְךָ עֲנִיִּים וְסוֹפְרִים וּמְלַמְּדֵי תִינוֹקוֹת אֶלָּא מִשִּׁמְעוֹן, כְּדֵי שֶׁיִּהְיוּ נְפוֹצִים
sources.says: Rashi says the poor, the scribes and the teachers of children come only from Simeon, so that they would be scattered.

sources.quote: והנה מצאנו כי גורל שמעון נפל בתוך נחלת בני יהודה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says we find that Simeon's lot fell inside Judah's inheritance.

49:8.headline: Judah: 'your brothers will יודוך you', a play on his name
49:8.body: Ibn Ezra says Jacob plays on the name: Judah is as his name says, and his brothers will praise him. Rashbam says יודוך is not 'praise' but 'make you king', from הוד, royal majesty.

sources.quote: יהודה אתה. כשמך וכן יודוך אחיך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says Judah, you are as your name, and so your brothers will praise you.

sources.quote: המפרש ישבחוך אחיך שטות הוא בידו
sources.says: Rashbam says that whoever explains it as 'your brothers will praise you' is making a mistake.

sources.quote: יודוך - ימליכוך. כמו יהודוך
sources.says: Rashbam says יודוך means they will make you king, like יהודוך.

49:8.headline: 'Sons of your father', not 'sons of your mother'
49:8.body: Rashi says Jacob said 'sons of your father' because the brothers came from several mothers, unlike Isaac's blessing of Jacob, which said 'sons of your mother'. Rashbam says the same.

sources.quote: עַל שֵׁם שֶׁהָיוּ מִנָּשִׁים הַרְבֵּה, לֹא אָמַר בְּנֵי אִמֶּךָ כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמַר יִצְחָק
sources.says: Rashi says because they were from many wives he did not say 'sons of your mother', as Isaac had said.

sources.quote: לפי שמארבע אמהות היו אמר: בני אביך
sources.says: Rashbam says that because they came from four mothers he said 'sons of your father'.

49:9.headline: 'From the prey, my son, you rose': a play on 'torn'
49:9.body: Rashi hears a play on 'torn apart' (טרף טרף) from Jacob's fear about Joseph: Judah rose above that suspicion. Ibn Ezra and Rashbam read it simply as prey taken from other creatures.

sources.quote: מִמַּה שֶׁחֲשַׁדְתִּיךָ בְּטָרֹף טֹרַף יוֹסֵף חַיָּה רָעָה אֲכָלָתְהוּ
sources.says: Rashi says it means from what I suspected you of, 'Joseph was surely torn by a wild beast'.

sources.quote: והטעם מטרף אחר, וזהו פשוטו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means from other prey, and that this is the plain sense.

sources.quote: והמפרשו במכירת יוסף לא ידע פשוטו של פסוק
sources.says: Rashbam says whoever explains it with the sale of Joseph does not know the plain sense of the verse.

49:10.headline: The 'scepter of Judah': exile leaders, or David's royal line?
49:10.body: Rashi says that after David the scepter means the heads of the exile in Babylon, who ruled by authority of the empire. Ibn Ezra says it is greatness, which stayed with Judah until David became king.

sources.quote: מִדָּוִד וָאֵילָךְ, אֵלּוּ רָאשֵׁי גָּלֻיּוֹת שֶׁבְּבָבֶל
sources.says: Rashi says from David onward, these are the heads of the exile in Babylon.

sources.quote: לא יסור שבט גדולה מיהודה עד שבא דוד
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the staff of greatness would not leave Judah until David came.

49:10.headline: 'The lawgiver from between his feet': scholars, or scribes?
49:10.body: Rashi says the lawgivers are the disciples, the princes of the Land of Israel. Ibn Ezra says a מחוקק is a scribe, who writes on a scroll sitting between his lord's feet.

sources.quote: הַתַּלְמִידִים, אֵלּוּ נְשִׂיאֵי אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל
sources.says: Rashi says the lawgivers are the students, the princes of the Land of Israel.

sources.quote: ופי' מחוקק. סופר, שיחוק על הספר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says מחוקק means a scribe, who inscribes on the scroll.

sources.quote: שכן דרך כל סופר להיות יושב בין רגלי הקצין
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is the custom for a scribe to sit between the feet of the official.

49:10.headline: What is 'Shiloh'? The Messiah, a city, or Rehoboam's coronation
49:10.body: Rashi, following Onkelos, says it means the King Messiah, with a midrash hearing 'a gift to him'. Ibn Ezra lists views including the city of Shiloh and a word for afterbirth, and Rashbam says Rehoboam came to Shiloh to restart the kingdom.

sources.quote: מֶלֶךְ הַמָּשִׁיחַ שֶׁהַמְּלוּכָה שֶׁלּוֹ, וְכֵן תִּרְגְּמוֹ אֻנְקְלוֹס. וּמִדְרַשׁ אַגָּדָה שִׁילוֹ – שַׁי לוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says it is the King Messiah, to whom the kingdom belongs, as Onkelos translates, and a midrash reads Shiloh as 'a gift to him'.

sources.quote: ויש מי שפי' אותו על עיר שילה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports that some explain it as the city of Shiloh.

sources.quote: עד כי יבא מלך יהודה הוא רחבעם בן שלמה שבא לחדש המלוכה בשילה
sources.says: Rashbam says until the king of Judah comes, namely Rehoboam son of Solomon, who came to renew the kingship at Shiloh.

49:10.headline: יקהת is a rare word for a gathering, from a dropped letter
49:10.body: Rashi says יקהת means a gathering of nations, from a root where the first letter drops, and Ibn Ezra links it to 'obedience of a mother' in Proverbs. Rashbam says the nations were those under Solomon.

sources.quote: ולו יקהת עמים. אֲסֵפַת הָעַמִּים
sources.says: Rashi says ולו יקהת עמים means the gathering of the nations.

sources.quote: ומלת יקהת. כמו "ליקהת אם"
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says יקהת is like 'obedience to a mother' in Proverbs.

sources.quote: קבוצת האומות שהיו כפופים תחת שלמה אביו
sources.says: Rashbam says it means the group of nations that were subject to Solomon his father.

49:10.headline: 'Until Shiloh comes' does not mean the scepter leaves then
49:10.body: Ibn Ezra says 'until' here does not mean the scepter leaves when Shiloh comes. It means 'until' in the sense of 'he will not lack bread until he has fields and vineyards', that is, the rule stays through that time and beyond.

sources.quote: ואין טעם עד כי יבוא שילה שיסור דשבט ממנו בבוא שילה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the meaning of 'until Shiloh comes' is not that the scepter leaves him when Shiloh comes.

49:11.headline: 'His ass's colt': a real donkey, or Jerusalem?
49:11.body: Rashi says it means a young donkey tied to a vine so loaded with grapes, and Onkelos reads it about the Messiah, with the vine as Israel and עירה as Jerusalem. Ibn Ezra links the word to 'thirty donkeys' in Judges.

sources.quote: אִישׁ יְהוּדָה יֶאֱסֹר לַגֶּפֶן עַיִר אֶחָד
sources.says: Rashi says a man of Judah would tie one donkey to a single vine.

sources.quote: גֶּפֶן – הֵם יִשְׂרָאֵל; עִירֹה – זוֹ יְרוּשָׁלַיִם
sources.says: Rashi reports Onkelos: the vine is Israel and עירה is Jerusalem.

sources.quote: עירה. כמו "על שלשים עירים"
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says עירה is like 'thirty donkey colts' in Judges.

49:11.headline: סותה: a rare word for a garment, linked to luring
49:11.body: Rashi says סותה is a kind of cloth, and that it hints at tempting, since a woman's dyed cloth can tempt a man. Ibn Ezra links it to a word for veil.

sources.quote: סותה. לְשׁוֹן מִין בֶּגֶד הוּא, וְאֵין לוֹ דִּמְיוֹן בַּמִּקְרָא
sources.says: Rashi says סותה is a kind of garment, with no similar word in Scripture.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן הֲסָתַת שִׁכְרוּת
sources.says: Rashi adds that the rabbis explained it as a word for being enticed to drunkenness.

sources.quote: והנכון בעיני שהוא מגזרת "מסוה"
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says he thinks it comes from the word for 'veil'.

49:11.headline: 'The son of his donkey': also 'they will build his house'
49:11.body: Rashi reads בני אתנו as 'son of his donkey', and also hears 'build': they will build his Temple, from the gate in Ezekiel. Ibn Ezra says the yod in בני is an added letter.

sources.quote: בני אתנו. יִבְנוּן הֵיכְלֵהּ, לְשׁוֹן שַׁעַר הָאִיתוֹן בְּסֵפֶר יְחֶזְקֵאל
sources.says: Rashi says בני אתנו means they will build his temple, from the gate in Ezekiel.

sources.quote: ויו"ד בני אתונו נוסף
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the yod in 'his donkey's son' is added.

49:12.headline: 'Eyes dark with wine': eyes, mountains, or springs?
49:12.body: Rashi says the plain sense is red eyes from much wine. In Onkelos' translation, עינים means mountains from which people see far, or springs.

sources.quote: אֲדֹם עֵינַיִם יְהֵא מֵרֹב יַיִן וּלְבֶן שִׁנַּיִם יְהֵא מֵרֹב חָלָב
sources.says: Rashi says the plain sense is eyes red from much wine and teeth white from much milk.

sources.quote: וּלְפִי תַרְגּוּמוֹ עֵינַיִם לְשׁוֹן הָרִים, שֶׁמִּשָּׁם צוֹפִים לְמֵרָחוֹק
sources.says: Rashi says by Onkelos' translation עינים means mountains from which people look far away.

49:12.headline: 'Teeth white from milk': teeth, or cliffs?
49:12.body: Rashi's plain reading is white teeth from milk, while Onkelos reads 'teeth' as the white rock of the hills. Ibn Ezra says it is named for the two rows of teeth.

sources.quote: תַּרְגּוּם שִׁנַּיִם, לְשׁוֹן שִׁנֵּי הַסְּלָעִים
sources.says: Rashi says the Aramaic translation of 'teeth' is the word for the crags of the rocks.

sources.quote: ולבן שנים. שם התואר ונקרא שנים על שם מערכות שנים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says שנים is named for the two rows of teeth.

49:13.headline: 'By the shore of seas': a coast, or a harbour for ships
49:13.body: Rashi says חוף is a border or coast, and that Zebulun's trade fed Issachar's Torah study. Ibn Ezra says it means a haven, from 'covering', as ships need shelter from the wind.

sources.quote: חוֹף, כְּתַרְגּוּמוֹ סְפָר
sources.says: Rashi says חוף is, as Onkelos translates, a border.

sources.quote: זְבוּלֻן עוֹסֵק בִּפְרַקְמַטְיָא וּמַמְצִיא מָזוֹן לְשֵׁבֶט יִשָּׂשכָר, וְהֵם עוֹסְקִים בַּתּוֹרָה
sources.says: Rashi says Zebulun did business and supplied food for Issachar's tribe, who studied Torah.

sources.quote: פי' לחוף מחוז והוא מגזרת "חופף עליו כל היום"
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says לחוף means a harbour, from 'covering over him all day'.

49:14.headline: 'A bony donkey': strong, burdened with Torah
49:14.body: Rashi says גרם means a donkey with strong bones, that carries the yoke of Torah, and Ibn Ezra says it means a donkey with heavy bone. Rashbam says it is a farmer, strong and well-built.

sources.quote: חֲמוֹר בַּעַל עֲצָמוֹת, סוֹבֵל עֹל תּוֹרָה
sources.says: Rashi says a donkey with bones, bearing the yoke of Torah.

sources.quote: דמהו לחמור שיש לו עצם כבד
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says he is likened to a donkey with heavy bone.

sources.quote: אלא עובד אדמתו יהיה כחמור בעל אברים חזק מצוי
sources.says: Rashbam says he will work his land, like a strong donkey with well-built limbs.

49:14.headline: 'Between the saddlebags': borders, rows, or city limits
49:14.body: Rashi says it means the boundaries between towns, where a donkey on the road lies down, and Rashbam says it means the city limits where fields are ploughed. Ibn Ezra says it means 'between the rows', or links it to 'You will establish peace for us' in Isaiah.

sources.quote: רוֹבֵץ בֵּין הַתְּחוּמִין, בִּתְחוּמֵי הָעֲיָרוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says it lies down between the boundaries, at the limits of the towns.

sources.quote: בין המשפתים. בין המערכות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says בין המשפתים means between the rows.

sources.quote: תחומי העיר לחרוש ולעבוד את האדמה
sources.says: Rashbam says it means the borders of the city, for ploughing and working the land.

49:15.headline: 'Bowed his shoulder to bear': the load of Torah, or war
49:15.body: Rashi says Issachar bowed his shoulder to bear the yoke of Torah, while Onkelos has him bear wars and conquer territory. Rashbam says it is the yoke of Israel's kings.

sources.quote: ויט שכמו לסבול עֹל תּוֹרָה
sources.says: Rashi says he bent his shoulder to bear the yoke of Torah.

sources.quote: ויט שכמו לסבול מִלְחָמוֹת וְלִכְבֹּשׁ מְחוֹזוֹת
sources.says: Rashi reports Onkelos' other reading: bent his shoulder to bear wars and conquer districts.

sources.quote: ויט שכמו לסבול - עול של מלכי ישראל
sources.says: Rashbam says it means the yoke of the kings of Israel.

49:15.headline: 'A labouring tax-payer': Torah rulings, or a plain tax
49:15.body: Rashi says Issachar's service was ruling on Torah law and setting the calendar. Ibn Ezra and Rashbam say Issachar simply paid tax to the king.

sources.quote: לִפְסֹק לָהֶם הוֹרָאוֹת שֶׁל תּוֹרָה וְסִדְרֵי עִבּוּרִין
sources.says: Rashi says it means to give them rulings of Torah and the order of the calendar.

sources.quote: והי' נותנים מס למלך ישראל שלא יצאו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says they gave tax to the king of Israel so as not to go out to war.

sources.quote: לתת למלכים עישור תבואותיו
sources.says: Rashbam says it means to give the kings a tenth of his produce.

49:16.headline: 'Dan will judge his people': is that about Samson?
49:16.body: The verse plays on the name Dan, 'judge'. Rashi says it means Dan will take revenge for his people, and was said of Samson, while Rashbam says that anyone who applies it to Samson has missed the deeper plain sense.

sources.quote: יִנְקֹם נִקְמַת עַמּוֹ מִפְּלִשְׁתִּים
sources.says: Rashi says he will take revenge for his people from the Philistines.

sources.quote: וְעַל שִׁמְשׁוֹן נִבָּא נְבוּאָה זוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says this prophecy was said about Samson.

sources.quote: המפרש על שמשון לא ידע בעומק פשוטו של מקרא כלל
sources.says: Rashbam says whoever explains it about Samson does not know the depth of the plain sense of the verse.

49:16.headline: 'Like one of the tribes of Israel': all Israel, or David?
49:16.body: Rashi says it means all Israel will be as one with Dan, or else that Dan is like the unique one among the tribes, David, who came from Judah. Ibn Ezra says Dan will be a standard-bearer, like the sons of the free wives.

sources.quote: וְעוֹד יֵשׁ לְפָרֵשׁ כאחד שבטי ישראל, כַּמְיֻחָד שֶׁבַּשְּׁבָטִים, הוּא דָּוִד
sources.says: Rashi gives a second reading: like the unique one among the tribes, who is David.

sources.quote: רמז שיהיה בעל דגל כאחד בני הגבירות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it hints that Dan will have a banner like one of the sons of the mistresses.

49:17.headline: שפיפן is found only here: a snake that strikes
